timeline.label: Dickens born in Portsmouth
timeline.detail: The family's later collapse into debt gave him the clerk's-eye view of London money that runs through the novella.

timeline.label: Poor Law Amendment Act
timeline.detail: The workhouse system Scrooge names so confidently when he is asked for a donation.

timeline.label: Dickens speaks in Manchester
timeline.detail: He addressed the Athenaeum there in October, on education and poverty, weeks before beginning the book.

timeline.label: A Christmas Carol published
timeline.detail: Chapman and Hall issued it on 19 December as a gift book with gilt edges and John Leech's illustrations; the production costs cut deeply into Dickens's profit.

timeline.label: Stage versions within weeks
timeline.detail: Edward Stirling's adaptation opened at the Adelphi Theatre in February, one of several unauthorised dramatisations.

timeline.label: Dickens publishes The Chimes
timeline.detail: Dickens follows the Carol with the second of five Christmas books, angrier and more directly political.

timeline.label: Dickens begins reading the Carol in public
timeline.detail: The first readings were given in Birmingham at the end of the year, and he went on performing an abridged text for the rest of his life.

timeline.label: Dickens dies at Gad's Hill
timeline.detail: By then the public readings had made Scrooge a role as much as a character.

timeline.label: R. W. Paul's film Scrooge; or, Marley's Ghost
timeline.detail: R. W. Paul's short film, among the earliest screen versions of any Dickens work.

timeline.label: Alastair Sim stars in the film Scrooge
timeline.detail: Brian Desmond Hurst's British film became one of the standard screen reference points for the part.

timeline.label: The Muppet Christmas Carol
timeline.detail: Brian Henson's film with Michael Caine keeps much of Dickens's narration by putting Gonzo on screen as the author.

books.title: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court
books.author: Mark Twain
books.written: 1885-89, in the years Twain was pouring his fortune into a typesetting machine that never worked

timeline.label: Twain born in Missouri
timeline.detail: In a slaveholding state, thirty years before emancipation; the slave chapters of this novel are written out of that childhood.

timeline.label: George Washington Cable gives Twain Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur
timeline.detail: George Washington Cable handed him Le Morte d'Arthur on tour, and the notebook joke about an itching knight followed within days.

timeline.label: First chapters read aloud
timeline.detail: Twain read the opening to an audience in Governor's Island and described the book as a contrast between two civilisations.

timeline.label: Twain pours money into the Paige typesetter
timeline.detail: He was pouring money into a machine of six thousand parts that never worked; the novel's faith in engineering was written by a man being ruined by it.

timeline.label: Later chapters written, including the slave gang and the sand-belt
timeline.detail: The later chapters, including the slave gang and the sand-belt, were written after the manuscript had been set aside twice.

timeline.label: First edition published by Charles L. Webster & Co.
timeline.detail: Charles L. Webster & Co. issued it in December with 220 illustrations by Dan Beard, whose drawings pushed the politics further than the text.

timeline.label: British edition published as A Yankee at the Court of King Arthur
timeline.detail: Chatto & Windus published it as A Yankee at the Court of King Arthur; English reviewers took the satire personally.

timeline.label: William Dean Howells praises the book in Harper's
timeline.detail: William Dean Howells praised the book's anger at privilege in Harper's, setting the terms for its American reception.

timeline.label: Twain's bankruptcy
timeline.detail: The typesetter failed and took his publishing house with it; he spent the next years on a lecture tour paying creditors.

timeline.label: First film version
timeline.detail: A silent adaptation began a century of screen versions that keep the eclipse and drop the sand-belt.

timeline.label: Film musical starring Bing Crosby
timeline.detail: The best-known adaptation turns the novel into a romance, which is a fair measure of how unbearable most readers find the ending.

timeline.label: Henrik Ibsen born at Skien
timeline.detail: His father's business failed when he was a boy, and money and social standing recur throughout his work.

timeline.label: Peer Gynt published
timeline.detail: The last of the great verse plays before Ibsen turned to contemporary prose drama.

timeline.label: Pillars of Society published
timeline.detail: The first of the modern prose plays, and the beginning of the sequence this play belongs to.

timeline.label: Et dukkehjem published in Copenhagen
timeline.detail: Published on 4 December in a first printing of 8,000 copies.

timeline.label: First performance at the Royal Theatre, Copenhagen
timeline.detail: On 21 December, with Betty Hennings as Nora.

timeline.label: Ibsen supplies an alternative ending for the German stage
timeline.detail: In it Nora does not leave; his letter of February 1880 explains that he wrote it himself only to stop somebody else doing it worse.

timeline.label: Ibsen's Ghosts published
timeline.detail: Often read as his reply to those who had wanted Nora to stay: a marriage nobody leaves, and what it costs.

timeline.label: First public British production
timeline.detail: At the Novelty Theatre, London, on 7 June, with Janet Achurch as Nora and Charles Charrington as Helmer, in William Archer's translation.

timeline.label: Ibsen returns to Norway
timeline.detail: After twenty-seven years living in Italy and Germany.

timeline.label: Ibsen dies in Kristiania
timeline.detail: By then his contemporary plays were established across Europe and had reshaped what a serious stage play could be about.

timeline.label: R. Farquharson Sharp's translation published
timeline.detail: Issued by J. M. Dent in Everyman's Library; it is the English text these quotations are checked against.

timeline.label: The play probably written
timeline.detail: Usually placed in the mid-1590s on stylistic grounds, close to Romeo and Juliet; no document fixes the year.

timeline.label: Francis Meres lists the play in Palladis Tamia
timeline.detail: The earliest external record that it existed, two years before it was printed.

timeline.label: First Quarto, printed for Thomas Fisher
timeline.detail: The title page says the play had been publicly acted by the Lord Chamberlain's Men. Most modern editions descend from this text.

timeline.label: Second Quarto, falsely dated 1600
timeline.detail: Set from Q1 and belonging to the group of reprints associated with Thomas Pavier.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies, from the second quarto, with small changes including the substitution of Egeus for Philostrate in the last act.

timeline.label: Samuel Pepys sees the play and detests it
timeline.detail: His diary records one of the bluntest hostile verdicts in the play's reception history.

timeline.label: Mendelssohn composes the overture
timeline.detail: Written when he was seventeen, and still the music most audiences hear in their heads.

timeline.label: Madame Vestris stages the play at Covent Garden
timeline.detail: A production that helped establish the Victorian fairy-spectacle tradition.

timeline.label: Mendelssohn's incidental music
timeline.detail: Added sixteen years after the overture, and the source of the wedding march.

timeline.label: Reinhardt and Dieterle's Hollywood film
timeline.detail: With James Cagney as Bottom and Mickey Rooney as Puck: the play as a studio fantasy.

timeline.label: Britten's opera premieres at Aldeburgh
timeline.detail: The libretto begins in the wood rather than in Athens, shifting the balance from law to enchantment.

timeline.label: Peter Brook's white box production for the RSC
timeline.detail: Sally Jacobs's bare white set, trapezes and circus skills replaced painted foliage and changed how the play could look.

timeline.label: Samuel Langhorne Clemens born in Florida, Missouri
timeline.detail: The family moved to Hannibal on the Mississippi four years later.

timeline.label: The Clemens family settles in Hannibal
timeline.detail: A river town in a slave state, and the model for St Petersburg in both Tom Sawyer and this book.

timeline.label: Clemens begins training as a Mississippi steamboat pilot
timeline.detail: Four years on the river gave him the geography, the vocabulary and eventually the pen name.

timeline.label: The Thirteenth Amendment abolishes slavery in the United States
timeline.detail: The novel is set roughly a generation earlier, but written and published well after emancipation, and in the middle of its reversal in the South.

timeline.label: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer is published, and Huck's manuscript is begun
timeline.detail: Twain wrote the first stretch at Quarry Farm near Elmira and then put it aside for years.

timeline.label: A brief return to the manuscript
timeline.detail: Work resumed and stalled again; the Grangerford and river material belongs to this uneven period.

timeline.label: Life on the Mississippi is published and the novel is finished
timeline.detail: A trip back down the river seems to have unlocked the second half, which was written quickly.

timeline.label: Chatto & Windus publish the British edition in December
timeline.detail: The London issue came out some weeks before the American one, partly to secure copyright.

timeline.label: Charles L. Webster & Company publish the American edition in February
timeline.detail: Twain's own subscription house, with illustrations by E. W. Kemble.

timeline.label: The Concord public library removes the book from its shelves
timeline.detail: The stated objections were to coarseness and bad grammar; Twain professed himself delighted by the sales it would bring.

timeline.label: Mark Twain dies at Redding, Connecticut
timeline.detail: By then the book was established, and the arguments about its last ten chapters had already begun.

timeline.label: Arthur Conan Doyle born in Edinburgh
timeline.detail: Into an Irish Catholic family; he took his medical degree at Edinburgh University.

timeline.label: Doyle enters the Edinburgh medical school
timeline.detail: There he encountered Dr Joseph Bell, whose habit of diagnosing a patient's trade and travels from their appearance is the acknowledged model for Holmes's method.

timeline.label: Holmes and Watson first appear, in A Study in Scarlet
timeline.detail: Holmes and Watson's first appearance, in Beeton's Christmas Annual, to very little notice.

timeline.label: Doyle's The Sign of the Four published
timeline.detail: The second novel, commissioned at a Lippincott's Magazine dinner in 1889 that also produced Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray.

timeline.label: The Strand Magazine begins the stories with 'A Scandal in Bohemia'
timeline.detail: 'A Scandal in Bohemia' appears with Sidney Paget's illustrations, and the magazine's circulation climbs with each number.

timeline.label: The twelve stories collected as a volume
timeline.detail: Published by George Newnes in October, in the order they had appeared.

timeline.label: Doyle kills Holmes at the Reichenbach Falls
timeline.detail: 'The Final Problem' closes the second series; readers cancelled subscriptions in numbers the magazine did not forget.

timeline.label: The Hound of the Baskervilles begins serialisation
timeline.detail: Set before the Falls, so that the detective could return without being resurrected.

timeline.label: Doyle brings Holmes back in 'The Adventure of the Empty House'
timeline.detail: 'The Adventure of the Empty House' explains the Reichenbach disappearance and restarts the series.

timeline.label: The last Holmes story published
timeline.detail: The Case-Book closes a sequence of fifty-six short stories and four novels written across forty years.

timeline.label: Doyle dies at Crowborough
timeline.detail: By then better known to himself for his spiritualist writings than for the detective.

timeline.label: Charles Lutwidge Dodgson born at Daresbury in Cheshire
timeline.detail: The eldest son of a clergyman, and the third of eleven children.

timeline.label: Dodgson is appointed Mathematical Lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford
timeline.detail: He held the post for a quarter of a century and lived in college for the rest of his life.

timeline.label: Dodgson first tells the story on a river trip, 4 July
timeline.detail: Dodgson tells the first version of the story to the three Liddell sisters on a boat trip towards Godstow.

timeline.label: Alice’s Adventures Under Ground given to Alice Liddell
timeline.detail: Written out and illustrated by Dodgson himself; the published book more than doubles it.

timeline.label: The first printing is withdrawn
timeline.detail: Tenniel objected to the quality of the reproduction of his illustrations.

timeline.label: The replacement impression reaches readers
timeline.detail: Dated 1866, this is the effective first published edition.

timeline.label: Through the Looking-Glass appears
timeline.detail: Published in December and dated 1872, again with Tenniel’s illustrations.

timeline.label: The Nursery ‘Alice’
timeline.detail: Carroll’s own shortened version for very young children, with coloured plates.

timeline.label: The last substantial revision of the text
timeline.detail: New settings incorporate Carroll’s final corrections to the standard wording.

timeline.label: Carroll dies at Guildford
timeline.detail: He died in January at his sisters’ house, The Chestnuts.

timeline.label: The book comes out of copyright in Britain
timeline.detail: New illustrated editions follow at once, among them Arthur Rackham’s.

timeline.label: The Under Ground manuscript comes to the British Museum
timeline.detail: Bought by American subscribers and presented to Britain; it is now British Library Add MS 46700.

timeline.label: Disney’s animated Alice in Wonderland
timeline.detail: It folds material from Through the Looking-Glass into Wonderland and fixes the book’s popular image for a century.

books.title: American Ghost Stories
books.author: F. Marion Crawford, Ambrose Bierce, Ellen Glasgow and others
books.written: Between 1878 and 1925, mostly for magazines and annuals, by ten writers of whom seven are women

timeline.label: Emma Frances Dawson's 'An Itinerant House' published
timeline.detail: Emma Frances Dawson's San Francisco story, the earliest in the collection.

timeline.label: F. Marion Crawford's 'The Upper Berth' published
timeline.detail: Crawford's story appears in The Broken Shaft, a Christmas annual dated 1886.

timeline.label: Ambrose Bierce's 'The Middle Toe of the Right Foot' published
timeline.detail: Bierce's story of the Manton house, later collected in Can Such Things Be? (1893).

timeline.label: Madeline Yale Wynne's 'The Little Room' in Harper's
timeline.detail: Madeline Yale Wynne's story in Harper's Magazine for August.

timeline.label: Mary Wilkins Freeman collects The Wind in the Rose-bush
timeline.detail: Freeman collects her supernatural stories, including The Shadows on the Wall, after their run in Everybody's Magazine.

timeline.label: Olivia Howard Dunbar's essay on the ghost in American fiction
timeline.detail: Olivia Howard Dunbar argues that the ghost has declined in American magazine fiction.

timeline.label: Olivia Howard Dunbar's 'The Shell of Sense' in Harper's
timeline.detail: Dunbar's own ghost story, in Harper's Magazine for December.

timeline.label: Ellen Glasgow's 'The Shadowy Third' in Scribner's
timeline.detail: Ellen Glasgow's nurse's story, in Scribner's Magazine.

timeline.label: Dorothy Scarborough's The Supernatural in Modern English Fiction
timeline.detail: Dorothy Scarborough publishes The Supernatural in Modern English Fiction.

timeline.label: Dorothy Scarborough's anthology Famous Modern Ghost Stories
timeline.detail: Scarborough's anthology, the copy-text here for Bierce and Dunbar.

timeline.label: Edith Wharton's 'Bewitched' in Pictorial Review
timeline.detail: Edith Wharton's story in Pictorial Review, the latest in the book.

timeline.label: Lucy Maud Montgomery born at Clifton, Prince Edward Island
timeline.detail: The village now called New London, a few miles from Cavendish.

timeline.label: Her mother dies; she is sent to her grandparents at Cavendish
timeline.detail: The household of an elderly couple and a child not quite their own is the one the novel rearranges.

timeline.label: Montgomery begins the novel
timeline.detail: She started writing in June, after months of what she called spade work on character and incident.

timeline.label: Contract with L. C. Page and Company
timeline.detail: Signed on 22 April, with the Boston firm that would publish the book and its sequels.

timeline.label: Anne of Green Gables published
timeline.detail: The first edition appeared in June; Montgomery recorded receiving her copies on the 20th.

timeline.label: First translation, into Swedish
timeline.detail: A Swedish edition appeared within a year, the beginning of an international readership.

timeline.label: Montgomery marries and leaves the Island
timeline.detail: She moved to Ontario as a Presbyterian minister’s wife, and wrote most of the Anne books away from Cavendish.

timeline.label: First film version
timeline.detail: A silent adaptation, now lost, made a decade after publication.

timeline.label: L. C. Page issues a reset and altered edition
timeline.detail: L. C. Page issued a newly set and slightly altered edition, which is why the 1908 printing matters as a base text.

timeline.label: Montgomery dies in Toronto
timeline.detail: She was buried at Cavendish, within sight of the landscape the novel renames.

timeline.label: The Canadian television adaptation
timeline.detail: Kevin Sullivan’s version fixed the novel’s appearance for a generation of readers and made Prince Edward Island a destination.

timeline.label: The battle of Actium
timeline.detail: Octavian's fleet defeats Antony and Cleopatra off the western coast of Greece. Shakespeare keeps the sea-fight offstage and stages the reaction to it instead.

timeline.label: The deaths of Antony and Cleopatra
timeline.detail: Alexandria falls to Octavian, and within the year both are dead. Plutarch's account of the manner of Cleopatra's death is the source Shakespeare follows most closely.

timeline.label: North's translation of Plutarch published
timeline.detail: Thomas North's English Plutarch, made from Amyot's French, gives Shakespeare both his narrative and some of his phrasing.

timeline.label: Mary Sidney's Antonius printed
timeline.detail: A translation of Robert Garnier's French tragedy, and part of an English fashion for closet drama about the Egyptian queen.

timeline.label: Samuel Daniel's Cleopatra published
timeline.detail: Written as a companion to Mary Sidney's play, and evidence that the subject was already established before Shakespeare took it up.

timeline.label: Julius Caesar first performed
timeline.detail: Antony's oration over the body belongs to the same Plutarchan material, seven or eight years earlier in Shakespeare's career.

timeline.label: Antony and Cleopatra most likely written
timeline.detail: Usually dated 1606–07, between King Lear and Coriolanus.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register
timeline.detail: The entry records an intention to print that produced no surviving quarto.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, printed among the tragedies with no act or scene divisions of the kind modern editions supply.

timeline.label: Dryden's All for Love published
timeline.detail: A rewriting of the story in neoclassical form, keeping the unities Shakespeare ignores; it held the stage for well over a century.

timeline.label: Lodge's Rosalynde published
timeline.detail: The prose romance that supplies almost all of the plot, including the wrestling, the disguise and the shepherds.

timeline.label: Christopher Marlowe killed at Deptford
timeline.detail: Phebe's 'Dead Shepherd' in 3.5 is the play's direct salute to him, and the line she quotes is his.

timeline.label: Marlowe's Hero and Leander published
timeline.detail: The poem Phebe quotes, and the source of the play's one open tribute to another writer.

timeline.label: The Globe opens on Bankside
timeline.detail: The theatre for which the play was almost certainly written, and the setting of the joke behind 'All the world's a stage'.

timeline.label: As You Like It most likely written
timeline.detail: Usually dated to 1599 or early 1600, close to Henry V and Julius Caesar.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register
timeline.detail: The entry orders publication to be stayed, and no quarto ever appeared.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, printed among the comedies.

timeline.label: Restored to the London stage
timeline.detail: After long neglect the play returned to the repertory at Drury Lane, and Rosalind became one of the great parts for an actress.

timeline.label: Paul Czinner's film
timeline.detail: With Elisabeth Bergner as Rosalind and Laurence Olivier as Orlando; the first sound film of the play.

timeline.label: All-male production at the National Theatre
timeline.detail: Directed by Clifford Williams, it revived the Elizabethan casting convention and reopened the argument about what the disguise means.

books.title: The Call of the Wild
books.author: Jack London
books.written: 1902, after London’s winter in the Yukon

timeline.label: Jack London born in San Francisco
timeline.detail: Born John Griffith Chaney; he took the surname of his stepfather, John London.

timeline.label: Gold found on a tributary of the Klondike
timeline.detail: The strike that emptied the Pacific ports of strong dogs the following summer.

timeline.label: London travels north to the Klondike
timeline.detail: He went in over the Chilkoot route in the first season of the stampede and wintered in the Yukon.

timeline.label: London returns to California
timeline.detail: He came back with almost no gold and with the material for the Northland stories that made his name.

timeline.label: The Call of the Wild serialised and published
timeline.detail: Five instalments in The Saturday Evening Post, then the Macmillan book, in a green pictorial binding with colour plates.

timeline.label: The argument about animal minds reaches the magazines
timeline.detail: Naturalists began attacking popular animal stories for granting their subjects human reasoning — a charge London would later answer directly.

timeline.label: White Fang published
timeline.detail: London called it a companion piece, reversing the journey: a wild dog brought into domestication.

timeline.label: London dies at Glen Ellen, California
timeline.detail: He was forty, and one of the first American writers to have made a large income from fiction alone.

timeline.label: First feature film adaptation
timeline.detail: Produced by Hal Roach and directed by Fred Jackman, beginning a century of screen versions.

timeline.label: William A. Wellman’s film with Clark Gable
timeline.detail: The studio version enlarges Thornton and adds a romance, a pattern most later adaptations follow.

timeline.label: Chris Sanders’s film with a digital Buck
timeline.detail: The animal is computer-generated throughout, which changes what a performance by Buck can be.

books.title: Carnacki, the Ghost-Finder
books.author: William Hope Hodgson
books.written: 1910-12, for The Idler and The New Magazine

timeline.label: Hodgson born in Essex
timeline.detail: A clergyman's son, and the second of twelve children.

timeline.label: Hodgson apprenticed to the sea
timeline.detail: Eight years afloat, including a Royal Humane Society medal for a rescue in heavy weather.

timeline.label: Hodgson opens a gymnasium in Blackburn
timeline.detail: He left the sea for physical culture, photography and lecturing; the practical streak in Carnacki comes from here.

timeline.label: Hodgson's first novel, The Boats of the Glen Carrig
timeline.detail: The Boats of the Glen Carrig, then The House on the Borderland the following year.

timeline.label: First five stories published in The Idler
timeline.detail: The Gateway of the Monster, The House Among the Laurels, The Whistling Room, The Horse of the Invisible and The Searcher of the End House.

timeline.label: The Thing Invisible published in The New Magazine
timeline.detail: The sixth case appears in The New Magazine, and is the most detective-like of them.

timeline.label: First book edition, published by Eveleigh Nash
timeline.detail: The six stories are published as a book.

timeline.label: Hodgson killed at Ypres
timeline.detail: A shell killed him in April, aged forty; he had re-enlisted after being invalided out.

timeline.label: Arkham House edition adds three more cases
timeline.detail: The Haunted Jarvee, The Find and The Hog are printed from manuscripts; later editions often run to nine cases.

timeline.label: Plautus writes the Menaechmi, about this time
timeline.detail: A Roman farce about identical twins separated as children, one of whom arrives in the city where the other lives.

timeline.label: Plautus printed at Venice
timeline.detail: Giorgio Merula's edition, the first in print, put the Latin comedies into circulation across Europe and in time into Elizabethan grammar schools.

timeline.label: Written, probably in the early 1590s
timeline.detail: Verse tests and the heavy use of rhyme group it with the earliest plays; no record survives of its first performance.

timeline.label: Played at Gray's Inn on 28 December
timeline.detail: Gesta Grayorum describes an evening of such disorder that the revels were remembered afterwards as the Night of Errors.

timeline.label: William Warner's English Menaechmi printed
timeline.detail: Entered in the Stationers' Register in June 1594. Shakespeare could read the Latin, so whether he used the translation is disputed.

timeline.label: Performed at court on 28 December
timeline.detail: A second festive-season record, ten years to the day after Gray's Inn, showing the play still in the company's repertory.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text. It prints among the Comedies as The Comedie of Errors, with no quarto behind it and few textual problems.

timeline.label: See If You Like It; or, 'Tis All a Mistake
timeline.detail: An anonymous two-act farce at Covent Garden, cut down from Plautus and Shakespeare together.

timeline.label: Thomas Hull's The Twins
timeline.detail: Hull's alteration was played at Covent Garden on 24 April 1762 and, so far as the bills show, not again; it survived in print.

timeline.label: Samuel Phelps at Sadler's Wells
timeline.detail: Phelps played the full text in place of the Georgian alterations; reviewers called it crude and extravagant, and the house laughed anyway.

timeline.label: The Boys from Syracuse opens on Broadway
timeline.detail: Rodgers and Hart's musical, directed by George Abbott, became the play's most successful afterlife and dropped its title entirely.

timeline.label: Trevor Nunn's RSC musical
timeline.detail: Music by Guy Woolfenden, lyrics by Nunn himself, choreography by Gillian Lynne, Judi Dench as Adriana; it transferred to the Aldwych and won the Olivier Award for Best New Musical.

timeline.label: North's translation of Plutarch's Lives
timeline.detail: Thomas North's English version of Amyot's French Plutarch, and the source Shakespeare follows most closely of any he ever used.

timeline.label: North's Plutarch reissued
timeline.detail: A second edition kept the Lives in print and in circulation through Shakespeare's Roman plays.

timeline.label: Shakespeare writes Julius Caesar
timeline.detail: The first of the plays taken from North, and the one that establishes Shakespeare's method of turning Plutarch's prose into verse.

timeline.label: Shakespeare writes Antony and Cleopatra
timeline.detail: Usually dated to 1606 or 1607, and the immediate predecessor of this play in the Roman sequence.

timeline.label: The Midland Revolt
timeline.detail: Risings against enclosure and grain shortage across the midland counties, often linked by scholars to the corn riot with which this play opens.

timeline.label: The play is written
timeline.detail: Generally dated around this year, which makes it Shakespeare's last tragedy.

timeline.label: The King's Men take the Blackfriars
timeline.detail: An indoor playhouse with a smaller, closer audience — a room in which a long silence between two actors can be made to work.

timeline.label: Plague closes the London playhouses
timeline.detail: A closure that ran on well into the following year and disrupted the company's plans for the new theatre.

timeline.label: The First Folio
timeline.detail: The play is printed first among the tragedies, from a manuscript whose stage directions are unusually full.

timeline.label: Boccaccio finishes the Decameron
timeline.detail: The ninth tale of the second day has a merchant wager on his wife's chastity and a rival win it by being carried into her bedroom in a chest.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles, second edition
timeline.detail: Shakespeare takes Cymbeline, Cassibelan and the quarrel over the Roman tribute from the British books, and reorders the reigns to suit himself.

timeline.label: The King's Men take the Blackfriars
timeline.detail: An indoor playhouse with descent machinery in the roof, of the kind the Jupiter scene asks for.

timeline.label: Cymbeline written
timeline.detail: Composed alongside Pericles, The Winter's Tale and The Tempest, at the end of Shakespeare's working life.

timeline.label: Simon Forman writes down what he saw
timeline.detail: His notebook records the wager, the man in the trunk and the cave in Wales. Forman died that September, so the play had been staged by then.

timeline.label: Printed in the First Folio
timeline.detail: No quarto survives. The Folio classes it as a tragedy and prints it last, closing the volume.

timeline.label: Played at court for Charles I
timeline.detail: The Master of the Revels recorded a performance by the King's players on New Year's Day, and noted that the king liked it.

timeline.label: D'Urfey rewrites it as The Injured Princess
timeline.detail: Thomas D'Urfey's version, subtitled The Fatal Wager, kept the stage in place of Shakespeare's text for the best part of a century.

timeline.label: Garrick brings the play back to Drury Lane
timeline.detail: David Garrick played Posthumus himself and returned something close to Shakespeare's text to the repertory.

timeline.label: Ellen Terry plays Imogen at the Lyceum
timeline.detail: Henry Irving took Iachimo. Bernard Shaw reviewed it, praised Terry and attacked almost everything else in the play.

timeline.label: Shaw rewrites the last act
timeline.detail: Cymbeline Refinished replaces the cascade of recognitions with a short scene in which Imogen is markedly less pleased to have her husband back.

timeline.label: The RSC makes Cymbeline a queen
timeline.detail: Melly Still's production cast Gillian Bevan as a ruling queen and set the British scenes in a shut-in, decaying country.

timeline.label: Luther's ninety-five theses at Wittenberg
timeline.detail: The university where Marlowe sets his play became the centre of the Reformation, and of its arguments about grace, faith and the freedom of the will.

timeline.label: A German magician called Faust dies, c. 1540
timeline.detail: A wandering astrologer and conjuror of that name is mentioned in several sixteenth-century German records. Almost nothing about him is certain, and the legend grew after his death.

timeline.label: Christopher Marlowe born in Canterbury
timeline.detail: The son of a shoemaker, baptised in February, two months before Shakespeare.

timeline.label: The fire-ship at Antwerp
timeline.detail: During the Prince of Parma's siege, an explosive ship wrecked his bridge across the Scheldt. Faustus wants 'stranger engines' than 'the fiery keel at Antwerp's bridge', which dates the speech after this event.

timeline.label: The German Faust book printed at Frankfurt
timeline.detail: The Historia von D. Johann Fausten, published by Johann Spies, gathered the legends into one cautionary life. In the same year Marlowe took his Cambridge MA and Tamburlaine reached the London stage.

timeline.label: Earliest surviving edition of the English Faust book
timeline.detail: The translation by 'P. F.' is Marlowe's direct source, down to the grapes and the horse-dealer. An earlier printing may have existed, which is one reason the play cannot be dated firmly.

timeline.label: Marlowe killed at Deptford
timeline.detail: Stabbed on 30 May, aged twenty-nine, days after being called before the Privy Council. None of his plays except Tamburlaine had yet been printed.

timeline.label: First recorded performances, at the Rose
timeline.detail: Philip Henslowe's diary lists the play in the Admiral's Men's repertory at the Rose from the autumn of this year. It was already an old play by then.

timeline.label: Henslowe pays for additions
timeline.detail: William Birde and Samuel Rowley received four pounds for 'adicyones in doctor fostes'. Whether their work survives in the 1616 text is still debated.

timeline.label: First quarto printed (the shorter A-text)
timeline.detail: The first quarto, the shorter version, and the one followed here.

timeline.label: Second, longer version printed (the B-text)
timeline.detail: A longer version with new comic and papal scenes, a softened vocabulary of oaths, and a title page showing Faustus in his conjuring circle.

timeline.label: Goethe's Faust, Part One
timeline.detail: Goethe's scholar is saved in the end. The contrast with Marlowe's has shaped how both are read.

timeline.label: Alexander Dyce's edition of Marlowe
timeline.detail: Dyce printed the 1604 and 1616 texts separately instead of blending them. His text of the 1604 quarto is the one used for every quotation here.

timeline.label: Thomas Mann's Doktor Faustus
timeline.detail: The pact retold as the life of a German composer, written in exile during and after the Second World War.

timeline.label: Oscar Wilde is born in Dublin
timeline.detail: Son of a surgeon and of the poet who wrote as Speranza.

timeline.label: Walter Pater’s Studies in the History of the Renaissance
timeline.detail: Its conclusion — to burn always with a hard, gem-like flame — is the argument Lord Henry repeats in a garden with the ethics removed.

timeline.label: Huysmans publishes A rebours
timeline.detail: The decadent French novel usually identified with the yellow-backed book Lord Henry sends; Wilde declined to confirm it.

timeline.label: The novel appears in Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine
timeline.detail: Thirteen chapters, printed in the July issue, and denounced in several London papers as a book for outlawed noblemen.

timeline.label: The revised book edition
timeline.detail: Published by Ward, Lock and Co. with six new chapters, a preface of aphorisms, and the James Vane plot added to give the second half a pursuer.

timeline.label: Wilde publishes Intentions and Lord Arthur Savile’s Crime
timeline.detail: Wilde’s most productive year as a prose writer, immediately before he turned to the stage.

timeline.label: The Importance of Being Earnest opens at the St James’s Theatre
timeline.detail: In February, with Wilde at the height of his fame and three months from the first trial.

timeline.label: The novel is used as evidence in court
timeline.detail: Passages were read out and Wilde was cross-examined on them during the libel action he brought against the Marquess of Queensberry.

timeline.label: De Profundis is written in Reading Gaol
timeline.detail: A long letter to Lord Alfred Douglas, and Wilde’s own account of a life lived for sensation.

timeline.label: Wilde dies in Paris
timeline.detail: At the Hôtel d’Alsace, aged forty-six, three years after his release.

timeline.label: Albert Lewin’s film for MGM
timeline.detail: Shot in black and white with the portrait revealed in colour — the best-known of many attempts to show what Wilde only describes.

timeline.label: Polidori’s The Vampyre is published
timeline.detail: Begun during the same 1816 Geneva summer as Frankenstein, and the story that made the vampire an aristocrat rather than a peasant revenant.

timeline.label: Bram Stoker is born in Dublin
timeline.detail: He was bedridden until about the age of seven, and later became an athlete at Trinity College.

timeline.label: Sheridan Le Fanu’s Carmilla appears in In a Glass Darkly
timeline.detail: A fellow Dubliner’s vampire novella, and the closest predecessor to Stoker’s handling of desire and illness.

timeline.label: Stoker becomes business manager of the Lyceum Theatre
timeline.detail: Twenty-seven years working for Henry Irving, whose stage presence is often heard behind the Count’s manners.

timeline.label: Stoker begins his working notes
timeline.detail: The surviving papers show a planned vampire novel taking shape before the name Dracula or the Transylvanian setting arrives.

timeline.label: Stoker spends the summer at Whitby
timeline.detail: The harbour, the abbey steps, the churchyard seat and the Russian schooner story all reached the novel from this visit.

timeline.label: Dracula published by Archibald Constable and Company
timeline.detail: A staged reading was given at the Lyceum in the same year, chiefly to secure the dramatic copyright.

timeline.label: Stoker dies in London
timeline.detail: He had written a dozen other novels, none of which is much read.

timeline.label: Murnau’s Nosferatu
timeline.detail: An unauthorised adaptation with the names changed; Stoker’s widow sued, and the court ordered the negatives destroyed.

timeline.label: Hamilton Deane’s authorised stage version opens
timeline.detail: At the Grand Theatre, Derby; the evening dress and the cloak with a standing collar are the play’s inventions, not the novel’s.

timeline.label: Universal’s Dracula with Bela Lugosi
timeline.detail: Adapted from the stage version rather than the book, and the reason most readers arrive expecting a very different Count.

books.title: Ethan Frome
books.author: Edith Wharton
books.written: Out of an earlier French exercise, Hiver, written while Wharton was living in Paris

timeline.label: Edith Newbold Jones born in New York
timeline.detail: Into the old moneyed society she would spend a career anatomising.

timeline.label: Marriage to Edward Robbins Wharton
timeline.detail: A match that became increasingly unhappy and ended in divorce in 1913.

timeline.label: The Mount completed at Lenox, Massachusetts
timeline.detail: Wharton designed the house and gardens herself and lived in the Berkshire hill country this book is set in.

timeline.label: A coasting accident at Lenox
timeline.detail: A documented sledding accident in the town, often connected with the novel's ending, though Wharton did not identify it as her source.

timeline.label: Wharton's The House of Mirth published
timeline.detail: The novel that made her reputation, and the first of her studies of a woman destroyed by an economy she is not allowed to work in.

timeline.label: Ethan Frome published
timeline.detail: By Charles Scribner's Sons, after appearing in Scribner's Magazine.

timeline.label: Wharton's The Custom of the Country published
timeline.detail: Published two years later, and as ruthless about money in drawing rooms as this book is about money on a hill farm.

timeline.label: Wharton's The Age of Innocence published
timeline.detail: Written after the war, from France, looking back at the New York of her childhood.

timeline.label: Wharton wins the Pulitzer Prize for The Age of Innocence
timeline.detail: The first woman to receive it, for The Age of Innocence.

timeline.label: Wharton dies in France
timeline.detail: At Saint-Brice-sous-Forêt, north of Paris, where she had lived for years.

timeline.label: Mary Wollstonecraft publishes A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
timeline.detail: The author’s mother, whose arguments about education and sympathy run through the creature’s narrative.

timeline.label: William Godwin publishes Political Justice
timeline.detail: The author’s father, and the source of the novel’s habit of testing obligation by argument rather than by feeling.

timeline.label: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin is born in London
timeline.detail: Her mother died within days, of complications following the birth.

timeline.label: Giovanni Aldini’s galvanic demonstrations in London
timeline.detail: Electrical experiments on the body of a hanged man at the Royal College of Surgeons, widely reported.

timeline.label: Mary Shelley begins the story at the Villa Diodati
timeline.detail: Byron proposes a ghost-story competition beside Lake Geneva; Shelley, then eighteen, begins the tale.

timeline.label: Frankenstein published anonymously in three volumes
timeline.detail: Dedicated to Godwin, with a preface written by Percy Bysshe Shelley, which led several reviewers to assume he was the author.

timeline.label: Presumption; or, The Fate of Frankenstein opens in London
timeline.detail: Richard Brinsley Peake’s version gives the creature no speech at all — the first of many adaptations to take his argument away.

timeline.label: A second edition names Mary Shelley as the author
timeline.detail: Published in two volumes while she was abroad, and seen through the press by her father.

timeline.label: The revised one-volume edition for Bentley’s Standard Novels
timeline.detail: Shelley adds the introduction about the Diodati summer and alters the novel’s account of Elizabeth, chance and fate. This is the text used here.

timeline.label: Mary Shelley dies in London
timeline.detail: She had outlived Percy Shelley by nearly thirty years and all but one of her children.

timeline.label: Edison Studios releases the first screen Frankenstein
timeline.detail: A single reel, long thought lost, in which the creature is produced in a vat rather than on a table.

timeline.label: James Whale’s Frankenstein for Universal
timeline.detail: Boris Karloff’s flat-headed, inarticulate creature becomes the popular image of a character who, in the novel, argues fluently for his rights.

timeline.label: Dickens born in Portsmouth
timeline.detail: Pip's childhood belongs roughly to the same decade as Dickens's own.

timeline.label: Dickens sent to work in a blacking warehouse
timeline.detail: Dickens's father was imprisoned for debt and the boy was sent out to work, an episode behind the novel's shame about hands, clothes and company.

timeline.label: Transportation to New South Wales ends
timeline.detail: The system that sent Magwitch to Australia, and the sentence he risks hanging by breaking.

timeline.label: David Copperfield completed
timeline.detail: Dickens re-read it before starting Great Expectations, to be sure he was not repeating himself in the first person.

timeline.label: Dickens moves to Gad's Hill Place
timeline.detail: In the Kent country the novel's marshes and estuary are drawn from.

timeline.label: Serialisation begins
timeline.detail: The first weekly instalment appeared in All the Year Round in December; Dickens took the novel on partly to lift the journal's sales.

timeline.label: The ending is changed
timeline.detail: Bulwer-Lytton read the manuscript ending and objected; Dickens wrote the replacement that has been printed ever since.

timeline.label: Serial ends and the book appears
timeline.detail: The last instalment ran in August, and Chapman and Hall published the novel in three volumes.

timeline.label: Dickens dies at Gad's Hill
timeline.detail: Great Expectations was his penultimate completed novel, followed by Our Mutual Friend.

timeline.label: David Lean's film
timeline.detail: Its graveyard opening and Satis House interiors have shaped how the novel is imagined ever since.

timeline.label: Alfonso Cuarón's film
timeline.detail: Relocated to Florida and New York, with Pip as a painter, which tests how much of the novel is the plot and how much the class system.

timeline.label: Mike Newell's film
timeline.detail: A return to period adaptation, with Ralph Fiennes as Magwitch and Helena Bonham Carter as Miss Havisham.

timeline.label: Jonathan Swift born in Dublin
timeline.detail: Educated at Kilkenny and Trinity College, Dublin, and later secretary to Sir William Temple.

timeline.label: The book’s date for Gulliver’s first voyage: 4 May 1699
timeline.detail: The fictional first voyage is dated 4 May 1699 — the book gives dates for every departure.

timeline.label: A Tale of a Tub and The Battle of the Books published
timeline.detail: Swift’s first sustained attack on false learning and modern authorship, and an anonymous one.

timeline.label: Swift installed as Dean of St Patrick’s, Dublin
timeline.detail: The post he held for the rest of his life, and the source of the name by which Ireland knew him.

timeline.label: Swift writes The Drapier’s Letters
timeline.detail: Swift’s campaign against Wood’s halfpence, written in the voice of a Dublin cloth merchant — another invented plain-speaking narrator.

timeline.label: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World published
timeline.detail: Benjamin Motte issues it in two volumes on 28 October, with Lemuel Gulliver on the title page.

timeline.label: Keys, sequels and imitations appear
timeline.detail: Explanatory ‘keys’, spurious continuations and parodies follow within months of publication.

timeline.label: Swift’s A Modest Proposal published
timeline.detail: The same deadpan applied to Irish famine, by a narrator whose arithmetic is as careful as Gulliver’s.

timeline.label: Faulkner’s Dublin edition
timeline.detail: The Travels appear in volume III of Swift’s collected works, with the letter to Sympson added.

timeline.label: Swift dies in Dublin
timeline.detail: He left the bulk of his estate to found a hospital for the mentally ill.

timeline.label: Fleischer Studios’ animated Gulliver’s Travels
timeline.detail: One of the best-known screen versions, and a clear case of the book surviving as Lilliput alone.

timeline.label: Television adaptation of all four voyages
timeline.detail: Unusually among adaptations, it keeps Part IV and Gulliver’s damaged return.

timeline.label: Saxo Grammaticus writes the Amleth story into the Gesta Danorum
timeline.detail: Composed around the turn of the thirteenth century: feigned madness, a murdered father and a dangerous uncle are all already there.

timeline.label: Belleforest retells Amleth in the Histoires tragiques
timeline.detail: The French version that carried the Danish story into sixteenth-century print and, in some form, to Shakespeare.

timeline.label: The Globe opens on Bankside
timeline.detail: The playhouse the Lord Chamberlain's Men built for themselves, and the theatre Hamlet was written for.

timeline.label: Hamlet most likely completed
timeline.detail: Usually dated to about 1599-1601, close to Julius Caesar and Twelfth Night.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register by James Roberts
timeline.detail: The entry precedes the first printing by a year.

timeline.label: The First Quarto printed
timeline.detail: Published by Nicholas Ling and John Trundle. Much shorter than the later texts, and differently ordered in places.

timeline.label: The Second Quarto printed
timeline.detail: Printed by James Roberts for Nicholas Ling, and advertised as enlarged; the longest of the early versions.

timeline.label: The First Folio text
timeline.detail: Prints material the Second Quarto lacks and omits material it has, so the two are witnesses rather than drafts.

timeline.label: Thomas Betterton plays Hamlet after the theatres reopen
timeline.detail: The beginning of the long tradition in which the part is treated as the measure of an actor.

timeline.label: Sarah Bernhardt plays Hamlet
timeline.detail: A reminder that the role has never been securely fixed to one kind of body or voice.

timeline.label: Laurence Olivier's film
timeline.detail: Heavily cut, and the first Shakespeare film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture.

timeline.label: Kenneth Branagh films a full-text Hamlet
timeline.detail: A four-hour screen version that keeps the material most productions have to lose.

timeline.label: Henry Percy, called Hotspur, is born
timeline.detail: He was in fact older than Henry IV, and old enough to be Hal's father; Shakespeare makes the two young men coevals so that they can be compared.

timeline.label: Henry Bolingbroke takes the crown
timeline.detail: The deposition staged in Richard II, and the debt the Percys come to collect in this play.

timeline.label: Richard II dies in captivity
timeline.detail: The death that the crusade to Jerusalem is meant to expiate, and that the new king never gets round to atoning for.

timeline.label: Hotspur defeats the Scots at Homildon Hill
timeline.detail: The victory whose prisoners he refuses to surrender in 1.3, which begins the quarrel.

timeline.label: The battle of Shrewsbury
timeline.detail: Fought on 21 July, and won by the king; the single combat between Hal and Hotspur is Shakespeare's invention.

timeline.label: Henry IV dies and Hal becomes Henry V
timeline.detail: Two plays later, and with Falstaff still expecting to be made an earl or a duke.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: The second edition is the play's principal quarry for the Percy rebellion and Shrewsbury.

timeline.label: The play is written and staged
timeline.detail: Usually dated to about this year, and probably in performance before it was entered for printing.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register and printed
timeline.detail: Andrew Wise entered it on 25 February; Peter Short printed the quarto, whose title page advertises Shrewsbury, Hotspur and the humorous conceits of Sir John Falstaff.

timeline.label: A second quarto, newly corrected
timeline.detail: The first of a string of reprints that make this the most frequently printed of Shakespeare's plays before the Folio.

timeline.label: The First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed as The First Part of Henry the Fourth, fixing the play inside the run from Richard II to Henry V.

timeline.label: Henry V succeeds his father
timeline.detail: Henry IV had taken the crown from Richard II in 1399, which is the fault the king prays about before Agincourt.

timeline.label: The Battle of Agincourt, 25 October
timeline.detail: Fought on Saint Crispin's Day after the siege of Harfleur and a long, sick march towards Calais.

timeline.label: The Treaty of Troyes
timeline.detail: Henry was recognised as heir to the French crown and married Katharine of Valois.

timeline.label: Henry dies; his infant son succeeds
timeline.detail: Henry VI was not yet a year old, which is the fact the Epilogue closes on.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's principal source for the campaign, alongside Edward Hall.

timeline.label: The Famous Victories of Henry the Fifth printed
timeline.detail: An anonymous earlier play covering the same career, which had already made the wild prince and the tennis balls familiar.

timeline.label: Henry V written and first performed
timeline.detail: The fifth Chorus's general returning from Ireland is almost certainly the Earl of Essex, who left in March and came home disgraced in September.

timeline.label: The first quarto
timeline.detail: About half the length of the Folio text, with no Chorus speeches and far less of the night-time debate among the soldiers.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The fuller text, and the basis of modern editions.

timeline.label: Laurence Olivier's film
timeline.detail: Made during the Second World War, and shaped throughout by that purpose: the Harfleur threat and the order to kill the prisoners are not in it.

timeline.label: Kenneth Branagh's film
timeline.detail: A muddier, more exhausted Agincourt, which restored much of what the 1944 version had removed.

timeline.label: Charlotte Brontë born at Thornton
timeline.detail: The family moved to Haworth parsonage four years later.

timeline.label: Charlotte is sent to school at Cowan Bridge
timeline.detail: Charlotte and three sisters were sent to the Clergy Daughters' School; the conditions there are generally taken to lie behind Lowood.

timeline.label: Maria and Elizabeth Brontë die
timeline.detail: Both fell ill at school and died at home within weeks of each other; Helen Burns is usually read as a memorial to Maria.

timeline.label: Poems by Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell
timeline.detail: The three sisters' first published book, which sold almost no copies and established the pseudonyms.

timeline.label: Jane Eyre published
timeline.detail: Smith, Elder and Co. brought it out in October in three volumes, as an autobiography edited by Currer Bell.

timeline.label: Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey appear
timeline.detail: Emily's and Anne's novels were published in December by Newby, partly on the strength of Jane Eyre's success.

timeline.label: Second edition, with a preface and a dedication to Thackeray
timeline.detail: Charlotte answered the charge of coarseness and dedicated the edition to Thackeray, not knowing about his own wife's confinement.

timeline.label: Note to the third edition
timeline.detail: Written to deny the rumour that all three Bells were one author.

timeline.label: Charlotte Brontë dies at Haworth
timeline.detail: She was the last of the six Brontë children, and died a few months after marrying Arthur Bell Nicholls.

timeline.label: Gaskell's Life of Charlotte Brontë
timeline.detail: The biography that fixed the Brontë legend, and shaped how Jane Eyre was read for a century.

timeline.label: Robert Stevenson's film
timeline.detail: With Joan Fontaine and Orson Welles; one of the versions that fixed Thornfield's visual style for later adaptations.

timeline.label: Wide Sargasso Sea
timeline.detail: Jean Rhys's novel gives Bertha Mason a childhood, a name of her own and a first-person voice, and has changed how Chapter 26 is read.

books.title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
books.author: Robert Louis Stevenson

timeline.label: Deacon William Brodie is hanged in Edinburgh
timeline.detail: A respected cabinetmaker and town councillor by day and a burglar by night; Stevenson grew up with the story and later wrote a play about him.

timeline.label: Robert Louis Stevenson is born in Edinburgh
timeline.detail: Into a family of lighthouse engineers, in a city of respectable New Town squares and old closes.

timeline.label: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species
timeline.detail: One source of the late-Victorian habit of describing the worse half of a man as an earlier one.

timeline.label: The novella is written at Bournemouth
timeline.detail: By Stevenson’s own account it began in a dream and was drafted at great speed; the household story that he burned a first version has been repeated ever since.

timeline.label: Published in London by Longmans, Green and Co.
timeline.detail: Issued as a cheap shilling shocker in January and taken up almost at once by pulpits and reviewers.

timeline.label: Stevenson's Kidnapped published
timeline.detail: Stevenson’s most productive period, and a reminder that the man writing about a divided self was also writing adventure fiction.

timeline.label: Richard Mansfield stars in the authorised stage version
timeline.detail: Thomas Russell Sullivan’s adaptation, first at the Boston Museum; the transformation is performed in front of the audience, reversing Stevenson’s method.

timeline.label: Mansfield brings the play to London during the Whitechapel murders
timeline.detail: The coincidence fixed a link between the story and the idea of a respectable Londoner who kills, and the production closed early.

timeline.label: Stevenson dies at Vailima in Samoa
timeline.detail: Aged forty-four, with Weir of Hermiston unfinished.

timeline.label: Rouben Mamoulian’s film for Paramount
timeline.detail: Fredric March won an Academy Award for the dual role, and the film’s subjective camera made the transformation the centrepiece.

timeline.label: Caesar assassinated in Rome
timeline.detail: On the ides of March, 44 BCE, in the meeting place at Pompey's theatre — the historical event behind Act III.

timeline.label: The battles at Philippi
timeline.detail: Brutus and Cassius are defeated by Antony and Octavius in Macedonia, some two years after the killing.

timeline.label: North's translation of Plutarch's Lives
timeline.detail: The English prose Shakespeare worked from, sometimes turning whole passages into verse with few changes.

timeline.label: The Globe opens, and the play is written
timeline.detail: Thomas Platter records seeing a tragedy of Julius Caesar at a Bankside playhouse on 21 September, with a dance after it.

timeline.label: First printed in the First Folio
timeline.detail: No quarto is known, which makes this one of the least textually disputed of the tragedies.

timeline.label: Orson Welles's modern-dress Caesar
timeline.detail: The Mercury Theatre staging in New York, cut and lit to read the play against contemporary European fascism.

timeline.label: Joseph L. Mankiewicz's film
timeline.detail: With Marlon Brando as Antony and John Gielgud as Cassius, and the funeral scene shot as a mass rally.

timeline.label: Gregory Doran's RSC production
timeline.detail: Set in a contemporary African state, with an all-Black cast, and later filmed.

timeline.label: John is crowned at Westminster
timeline.detail: Richard I dies childless and the crown passes to his youngest brother, over the claim of Geoffrey's son Arthur.

timeline.label: Arthur of Brittany is captured at Mirebeau
timeline.detail: Taken by John's forces while besieging his own grandmother Eleanor, he was imprisoned at Falaise and then Rouen, and was never seen again after April 1203.

timeline.label: John surrenders the kingdom to the papal legate
timeline.detail: After four years of excommunication he accepted Stephen Langton and received England back from Pandulph as a papal fief.

timeline.label: Magna Carta is sealed at Runnymede
timeline.detail: The event that now defines the reign, and the one the play leaves out entirely.

timeline.label: Louis of France lands in England; John dies at Newark
timeline.detail: The barons invited the Dauphin over; John lost his baggage train in the Wash and died of dysentery in October, and was buried at Worcester.

timeline.label: The Troublesome Reign of King John is printed
timeline.detail: An anonymous two-part play with the same unusual sequence of events, generally taken as the source Shakespeare worked from.

timeline.label: Shakespeare writes King John
timeline.detail: Dated to the middle of the 1590s on style and on its place among the other histories.

timeline.label: Francis Meres lists it in Palladis Tamia
timeline.detail: His roll-call of Shakespeare's plays names King John, which fixes the latest possible date of composition.

timeline.label: The First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text. It opens the section of histories, ahead of Richard II.

timeline.label: Two rival King Johns in London
timeline.detail: Garrick played the king at Drury Lane against Colley Cibber's adaptation Papal Tyranny at Covent Garden, during the year of the Jacobite rising.

timeline.label: Charles Kemble's antiquarian revival
timeline.detail: J. R. Planche's researched thirteenth-century costumes at Covent Garden began the fashion for historically accurate Shakespeare staging.

timeline.label: Herbert Beerbohm Tree's production
timeline.detail: A spectacular staging at Her Majesty's Theatre, from which a short filmed fragment survives, often called the earliest Shakespeare film.

timeline.label: The second edition of Holinshed's Chronicles
timeline.detail: Carries the story of King Leir and his three daughters, drawn from Geoffrey of Monmouth, with a restoration that Shakespeare removes.

timeline.label: Sidney's Arcadia
timeline.detail: Supplies the blinded father and the wronged son that Shakespeare builds into the Gloucester plot.

timeline.label: The anonymous King Leir performed
timeline.detail: An older, more openly Christian play on the same story; printed in 1605, and probably known to Shakespeare.

timeline.label: Harsnett's Declaration of Egregious Popish Impostures
timeline.detail: The source of the fiends Poor Tom names, and evidence that the play was written after it appeared.

timeline.label: Performed before King James at Whitehall
timeline.detail: The Stationers' Register record and the quarto title page both point to St Stephen's night in the Christmas holidays.

timeline.label: The First Quarto printed
timeline.detail: Printed for Nathaniel Butter as a True Chronicle Historie, and linking the play to the King's Men at the Globe.

timeline.label: Second Quarto, falsely dated 1608
timeline.detail: A reprint that keeps the 1608 date on its title page; its true year was not established until the twentieth century.

timeline.label: The First Folio text
timeline.detail: Printed as The Tragedie of King Lear, with over a hundred lines the quarto lacks and around three hundred fewer of the quarto's.

timeline.label: Nahum Tate's History of King Lear
timeline.detail: Removes the Fool, marries Cordelia to Edgar and lets Lear live. It held the English stage for more than a century.

timeline.label: Macready restores the Fool and the tragic ending
timeline.detail: Priscilla Horton played the restored Fool; Shakespeare's ending returned to public stage memory.

timeline.label: Peter Brook's film
timeline.detail: Made from his 1962 Stratford production, with Paul Scofield as Lear and almost every trace of comfort stripped out.

timeline.label: Trevor Nunn's RSC production with Ian McKellen
timeline.detail: A stormy, thrust-stage staging that included an on-stage hanging of the Fool.

timeline.label: A French embassy visits the real Navarre
timeline.detail: Catherine de’ Medici and her daughter Marguerite de Valois travelled to Henri of Navarre’s court at Nérac with a train of ladies, to settle the terms of Marguerite’s dowry and the disputed lands of the south-west. The play’s situation is this visit with the politics kept and the outcome changed.

timeline.label: English troops fight beside Navarre’s commanders
timeline.detail: Essex took an English force to Normandy in support of Henri of Navarre. The Duc de Biron, the Duc de Longueville and the Duc de Mayenne were named in the newsbooks that came back, and Shakespeare gave three of them to the lords of the academy.

timeline.label: The play written
timeline.detail: The rhyming, the sonnets set into the dialogue and the density of the wordplay place it beside A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Romeo and Juliet in the middle of the 1590s. No document records a first performance.

timeline.label: Presented before the Queen at Christmas
timeline.detail: The title page of the following year’s quarto says the comedy was presented before her Highness the last Christmas, which puts a court performance in the holiday season of 1597 and 1598.

timeline.label: The first quarto printed
timeline.detail: William White printed it for the bookseller Cuthbert Burby, describing it as newly corrected and augmented, with Shakespeare’s name on the title page. It is the only substantive early text: the Folio was set from a copy of it.

timeline.label: Francis Meres names it
timeline.detail: Palladis Tamia lists Love’s Labour’s Lost among the comedies that show Shakespeare most excellent, alongside a title, Love’s Labour’s Won, that nobody has since identified.

timeline.label: Robert Tofte reports seeing it played
timeline.detail: The poem Alba: The Months Minde of a Melancholy Lover describes watching Love’s Labour’s Lost and finding the comedy painful to sit through as a man in love. It is the earliest response to a performance by anyone in the audience.

timeline.label: Revived for Queen Anne
timeline.detail: Sir Walter Cope wrote to Robert Cecil in January that Burbage knew of no new play the Queen had not seen, but that the company had revived an old one called Love’s Labour’s Lost, which for wit and mirth he thought would please her exceedingly.

timeline.label: Printed in the First Folio
timeline.detail: Heminges and Condell placed it among the comedies, in a text set from the 1598 quarto. The Folio keeps the quarto’s duplicated passages in Act IV and Act V, where an earlier and a revised version of the same speech both stand.

timeline.label: A second quarto
timeline.detail: John Smethwick published a fresh quarto, printed from the Folio text. After this the play disappears from the record of performance for two hundred years.

timeline.label: Madame Vestris revives it at Covent Garden
timeline.detail: The first recorded professional production since the reign of James I. It ran briefly and was not much liked, and the comedy kept its reputation as an early experiment too clever to play.

timeline.label: Peter Brook’s production at Stratford
timeline.detail: Brook set the play in the world of Watteau, with Paul Scofield as Armado, and made Marcadé’s entrance the hinge of the evening. The production is generally credited with returning the comedy to the regular repertory.

books.title: Lyrical Ballads
books.author: William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge
books.written: Mostly between March and July 1798, on and around the Quantock Hills, with The Ancyent Marinere begun on a walk in November 1797

timeline.label: Wordsworth and Coleridge meet
timeline.detail: Introduced in Bristol; within two years they were living four miles apart in Somerset.

timeline.label: The Wordsworths move to Alfoxden, near Coleridge
timeline.detail: The Wordsworths take Alfoxden House, a walk from Coleridge's cottage at Nether Stowey. Most of the book is written in the twelve months that follow.

timeline.label: Coleridge begins The Ancyent Marinere on a walk
timeline.detail: Planned in November on a walk towards Lynton, partly to pay for the trip; a friend's dream of a skeleton ship and a sailor's account of albatrosses went into it.

timeline.label: Tintern Abbey composed
timeline.detail: Written in July, in Wordsworth's head, on the walk back to Bristol from the Wye, and set down on arrival.

timeline.label: First edition published anonymously
timeline.detail: Joseph Cottle issues five hundred copies in Bristol in September with neither poet named.

timeline.label: Southey's hostile review in the Critical Review
timeline.detail: In the Critical Review he calls the Marinere a Dutch attempt at German sublimity, and the volume's best-known poem is written off at once.

timeline.label: Wordsworth and Coleridge leave for Germany
timeline.detail: The two poets leave for Goslar and Ratzeburg; the separation ends the year of daily collaboration.

timeline.label: The second edition
timeline.detail: Two volumes, Wordsworth's name alone on the title page, Michael and the Lucy poems added, the Marinere respelled and moved out of first place.

timeline.label: The Preface expanded
timeline.detail: Wordsworth adds the definitions the book is now remembered by, including poetry as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings.

timeline.label: Coleridge disputes the Preface in Biographia Literaria
timeline.detail: Biographia Literaria devotes two chapters to disputing Wordsworth's theory of poetic diction while praising the poems it produced.

timeline.label: Wordsworth cuts the mocked couplet from The Thorn
timeline.detail: Wordsworth finally cuts the three-feet-long couplet from The Thorn after twenty years of ridicule.

books.title: M. R. James: Collected Ghost Stories
books.author: M. R. James
books.written: Between 1893 and 1936, most of them read aloud to friends at Christmas before they were printed

timeline.label: M. R. James born in Kent
timeline.detail: The son of an Evangelical clergyman; he grew up in the Suffolk village of Great Livermere, which stands behind several of the stories.

timeline.label: M. R. James goes up to King's College, Cambridge
timeline.detail: He arrived as an undergraduate and stayed for most of his life, becoming Provost in 1905.

timeline.label: First two stories read aloud at Cambridge
timeline.detail: Canon Alberic's Scrap-book and Lost Hearts were read aloud to friends at King's; the form was oral before it was printed.

timeline.label: M. R. James publishes his first manuscript catalogue
timeline.detail: His catalogues of medieval manuscripts in Cambridge libraries are still in use, and supply the fiction's furniture.

timeline.label: Ghost Stories of an Antiquary published
timeline.detail: Eight stories published by Edward Arnold, with a preface naming the real settings.

timeline.label: More Ghost Stories of an Antiquary published
timeline.detail: Casting the Runes and The Tractate Middoth among them; the second volume is where the method is at its most confident.

timeline.label: A Thin Ghost and Others published
timeline.detail: Five stories written during and after the war, drier and bleaker than the earlier work.

timeline.label: A Warning to the Curious published
timeline.detail: The title story, about a buried crown on the Suffolk coast, is the one many readers put first.

timeline.label: The Collected Ghost Stories published
timeline.detail: Everything gathered in one volume, with four stories added; the book has never been out of print since.

timeline.label: M. R. James dies at Eton
timeline.detail: His last piece appeared in The London Mercury in the year he died.

timeline.label: Jonathan Miller's BBC film Whistle and I'll Come to You
timeline.detail: Jonathan Miller's television film fixed the stories in British Christmas viewing, and the BBC adaptations continued for decades.

timeline.label: The historical Macbeth becomes king of Alba
timeline.detail: He ruled for seventeen years, a reign Shakespeare compresses to a few violent months.

timeline.label: The historical Macbeth is killed at Lumphanan
timeline.detail: Not at Dunsinane, and not by Macduff.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's chief source for the Scottish material, including the meeting with the three weird sisters.

timeline.label: James VI publishes Daemonologie
timeline.detail: The future king of England writes a dialogue on witchcraft six years before inheriting the English throne.

timeline.label: James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England
timeline.detail: A Scottish king in London, claiming descent from Banquo, changes what a Scottish play on a London stage can mean.

timeline.label: The Gunpowder Plot
timeline.detail: The conspiracy and its trials put the word equivocation into everyday London use.

timeline.label: Macbeth most likely written and first performed
timeline.detail: The Porter's equivocator is the strongest internal evidence for the date.

timeline.label: Simon Forman records seeing Macbeth at the Globe
timeline.detail: The earliest surviving eyewitness account of the play in performance.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early printed text of the play, and a short one.

timeline.label: Verdi's Macbeth premieres in Florence
timeline.detail: Revised for Paris in 1865, it becomes a performance tradition of its own.

timeline.label: Orson Welles directs the Federal Theatre Project's Black-cast Macbeth
timeline.detail: Staged at the Lafayette Theatre in Harlem and relocated to a Caribbean island.

timeline.label: Cinthio's Hecatommithi
timeline.detail: The collection containing the Epitia story, in which the sister yields to the magistrate and the brother is executed anyway.

timeline.label: George Whetstone's Promos and Cassandra
timeline.detail: A two-part English play on the same material, and Shakespeare's nearest model in his own language.

timeline.label: James VI's Basilikon Doron
timeline.detail: The king's own book of advice on rule, reprinted in London in 1603; its arguments about how a prince should hold himself were fresh when this play was written.

timeline.label: James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England
timeline.detail: A new ruler with known views on justice, clemency and the private conduct of magistrates.

timeline.label: Plague closes the London playhouses
timeline.detail: A long closure that pushed the King's Men out to the provinces and back to court performance.

timeline.label: The play is written
timeline.detail: Usually dated to this year, alongside Othello and the other so-called problem plays.

timeline.label: First recorded performance at court
timeline.detail: Played on 26 December during the Christmas season, before James I.

timeline.label: The Act to Restrain Abuses of Players
timeline.detail: Oaths and holy names were legislated off the public stage, one reason Folio texts of the period can differ from what was first spoken.

timeline.label: The First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text of the play, printed among the comedies.

timeline.label: Davenant's The Law Against Lovers
timeline.detail: A Restoration adaptation that grafted Beatrice and Benedick onto this plot and gave the ending the romance the original withholds.

timeline.label: Herman Melville born in New York
timeline.detail: His father's business failed and died with him, and Melville's formal schooling ended early.

timeline.label: The whaleship Essex is sunk by a sperm whale
timeline.detail: Owen Chase's narrative of the wreck and its aftermath became one of the novel's central sources.

timeline.label: J. N. Reynolds publishes an account of Mocha Dick
timeline.detail: A white sperm whale of the Pacific, already famous in maritime print before Melville named one.

timeline.label: Melville sails from Fairhaven on the whaler Acushnet
timeline.detail: He deserted in the Marquesas eighteen months later, which gave him the material for his first book.

timeline.label: Typee makes him briefly famous
timeline.detail: A South Seas narrative sold as fact; the reading public wanted more of the same from him for the rest of his life.

timeline.label: Melville moves to Arrowhead and meets Hawthorne
timeline.detail: The book he was already writing grew considerably longer and stranger during the friendship.

timeline.label: Published as The Whale in London and Moby-Dick in New York
timeline.detail: The London issue was expurgated, ran to three volumes, and omitted the epilogue, so its reviewers met a narrator who appeared not to have survived.

timeline.label: Pierre is published and the reviews turn hostile
timeline.detail: Melville's reputation as a writer of readable sea adventures did not survive the two books together.

timeline.label: Melville dies in New York
timeline.detail: He had spent nearly twenty years as a customs inspector on the docks, and left Billy Budd unpublished.

timeline.label: Raymond Weaver's biography opens the Melville revival
timeline.detail: The first full life of the writer, published thirty years after his death, made the case that the neglected books were the important ones.

timeline.label: Rockwell Kent's illustrated edition
timeline.detail: His black-and-white designs shaped how a generation of readers pictured the ship and the whale.

timeline.label: John Huston's film, written with Ray Bradbury
timeline.detail: Gregory Peck as Ahab fixed the popular version of the story as a chase with the cetology cut out.

books.title: Mrs Dalloway
books.author: Virginia Woolf
books.written: 1922–24, partly out of an earlier short story

timeline.label: Virginia Stephen born in Kensington
timeline.detail: Into a large literary household; her father Leslie Stephen edited the Dictionary of National Biography.

timeline.label: Her mother dies
timeline.detail: The first of the bereavements that were followed by breakdowns, and the beginning of her own long history with doctors.

timeline.label: The Voyage Out published
timeline.detail: Her first novel, in which a Mr and Mrs Dalloway appear as passengers.

timeline.label: The Hogarth Press founded
timeline.detail: Set up by Leonard and Virginia Woolf with a hand press, which eventually meant she published herself and answered to no editor.

timeline.label: The Armistice
timeline.detail: Less than five years before the June day in 1923 that the novel describes, and still the event everybody in it is organised around.

timeline.label: Jacob's Room published
timeline.detail: The first of her novels to abandon conventional plotting, and the book that made this one possible.

timeline.label: The War Office committee on shell-shock reports
timeline.detail: Its evidence and recommendations were argued over publicly while Woolf was writing Septimus.

timeline.label: 'Mrs Dalloway in Bond Street' appears
timeline.detail: The short story out of which the novel grew, and which supplied its opening walk.

timeline.label: Mrs Dalloway published on 14 May
timeline.detail: By the Hogarth Press, with a jacket designed by Vanessa Bell.

timeline.label: Woolf's The Common Reader published
timeline.detail: Her first collection of essays, which set out in criticism the case her fiction was making in practice.

timeline.label: Woolf's To the Lighthouse published
timeline.detail: The next novel, which takes the method of this one and stretches it across ten years and one empty house.

timeline.label: Woolf drowns herself in the River Ouse
timeline.detail: At fifty-nine, in Sussex, during the second war.

timeline.label: Ariosto's Orlando Furioso first published
timeline.detail: Its story of Ginevra, falsely accused after a maid is seen at her window in her mistress's clothes, is the closest analogue to the Hero plot.

timeline.label: Bandello's Novelle
timeline.detail: Another version of the slandered bride, set in Messina, which brings the story to the city Shakespeare uses.

timeline.label: Sir John Harington translates Orlando Furioso
timeline.detail: The English verse translation makes the Ginevra episode available to readers and playwrights in London.

timeline.label: The play is most likely written
timeline.detail: Composition is usually placed in 1598 or 1599, at the end of the decade of comedies.

timeline.label: First Quarto
timeline.detail: Printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise and William Aspley; its title page links the play to the Lord Chamberlain's Men.

timeline.label: Performed at court
timeline.detail: Recorded among the plays given during the celebrations for the marriage of Princess Elizabeth.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies, with some of the quarto's confusing speech prefixes regularised.

timeline.label: Peggy Ashcroft and John Gielgud at Stratford
timeline.detail: The pairing that began the modern tradition of the play as a vehicle for two major actors.

timeline.label: Judi Dench and Donald Sinden for the RSC
timeline.detail: One of the best remembered of the company's many Beatrice and Benedick pairings.

timeline.label: Kenneth Branagh's film
timeline.detail: Shot at the Villa Vignamaggio in Tuscany, with Emma Thompson as Beatrice; one of the most commercially successful Shakespeare films.

timeline.label: Iqbal Khan sets the play in contemporary Delhi
timeline.detail: An RSC production with Meera Syal as Beatrice, staged as part of the World Shakespeare Festival.

timeline.label: Kenny Leon's Public Theater production is filmed
timeline.detail: An all-Black cast in a contemporary American political setting, recorded for broadcast.

books.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
books.author: Frederick Douglass
