timeline.label: Douglass born Frederick Bailey in Talbot County, Maryland
timeline.detail: The date is now generally given as February 1818, though the book opens by saying he has never seen a record of it.

timeline.label: Sent from the Eastern Shore to Baltimore
timeline.detail: He was about eight. The move put him in Hugh and Sophia Auld's house, where the lessons began.

timeline.label: The fight with Edward Covey
timeline.detail: Dated in the book to one of the hottest days of August, after six months of being hired out to a man paid in labour to break people.

timeline.label: Escape to New York, and marriage to Anna Murray
timeline.detail: The book gives the marriage certificate in full and says nothing whatever about the journey.

timeline.label: First speech to a white audience, at Nantucket
timeline.detail: On 11 August, at an anti-slavery convention; Garrison's preface begins from that meeting.

timeline.label: The Narrative published in Boston
timeline.detail: Issued by the Anti-Slavery Office with Garrison's preface and Wendell Phillips's letter attached.

timeline.label: British supporters purchase his legal freedom
timeline.detail: Raised during a lecture tour of Britain and Ireland undertaken partly because the book had made him traceable.

timeline.label: Douglass founds The North Star in Rochester
timeline.detail: His own paper, and the beginning of his separation from Garrison's wing of the movement.

timeline.label: Douglass publishes My Bondage and My Freedom
timeline.detail: A longer second autobiography, written without a white sponsor's preface and less willing to be a specimen.

timeline.label: The Emancipation Proclamation
timeline.detail: Douglass recruited for the Union army and pressed Lincoln on the pay and treatment of black soldiers.

timeline.label: Douglass publishes Life and Times of Frederick Douglass
timeline.detail: The third autobiography, which finally describes how the escape was made.

timeline.label: Douglass dies in Washington
timeline.detail: On 20 February, after a lifetime of public office, journalism and speaking.

timeline.label: Cinthio's Hecatommithi published
timeline.detail: The Italian story collection containing the tale of the Moor, the ensign and the handkerchief.

timeline.label: Venice loses Cyprus to the Ottomans
timeline.detail: The island Shakespeare's garrison defends had been Ottoman for a generation by the time the play was written.

timeline.label: Knolles's General History of the Turks
timeline.detail: Evidence of how current Ottoman affairs were in London when the play was taking shape.

timeline.label: First recorded performance at Whitehall
timeline.detail: The Revels accounts place the Moor of Venice at court on 1 November.

timeline.label: Parliament restrains profanity on the stage
timeline.detail: Often connected with the Folio text's removal of oaths that the quarto prints.

timeline.label: The First Quarto printed
timeline.detail: Printed by Nicholas Okes for Thomas Walkley; its title page records performance at the Globe and Blackfriars.

timeline.label: The First Folio text
timeline.detail: Around 160 lines longer than the quarto, including the Willow Song and the Pontic sea speech.

timeline.label: Desdemona and the first professional actress
timeline.detail: Restoration records associate the part with the first appearance of a woman on the English public stage.

timeline.label: Henry Irving plays Iago to Edwin Booth's Othello
timeline.detail: A London season that fixed the two parts as a pair of star roles for a generation.

timeline.label: Orson Welles's film
timeline.detail: Shot over several years and edited into a fragmented, architectural version of the tragedy.

timeline.label: Oliver Parker's film
timeline.detail: Laurence Fishburne as Othello and Kenneth Branagh as Iago, with Iago speaking directly to camera.

timeline.label: Iqbal Khan's RSC production
timeline.detail: Hugh Quarshie as Othello and Lucian Msamati as the first Black actor to play Iago at the RSC.

books.title: Paradise Lost
books.author: John Milton
books.written: Composed largely in the 1650s and early 1660s, by dictation

timeline.label: John Milton born in Bread Street, London
timeline.detail: The son of a scrivener and composer, in a household that could afford tutors and music.

timeline.label: Milton travels in Italy
timeline.detail: He later wrote of having visited the aged Galileo, then a prisoner of the Inquisition; Galileo's telescope appears in the poem.

timeline.label: Areopagitica published
timeline.detail: His argument against pre-publication licensing turns on the claim that a virtue never tested is no virtue — the position Eve takes in Book IX.

timeline.label: Charles I executed; Milton defends the regicide in print
timeline.detail: The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates appears within weeks, and Milton is appointed Secretary for Foreign Tongues to the Council of State.

timeline.label: Milton is completely blind
timeline.detail: From this point everything he writes is dictated, including the whole of the epic.

timeline.label: The Restoration
timeline.detail: Milton goes into hiding, is arrested and released; his defences of the regicide are burnt by the hangman.

timeline.label: Plague drives Milton out of London
timeline.detail: He took a cottage at Chalfont St Giles in Buckinghamshire, where work on the poem continued.

timeline.label: Paradise Lost published in ten books
timeline.detail: Printed in London the year after the Great Fire, with a contract paying Milton five pounds down.

timeline.label: Paradise Regained and Samson Agonistes published together
timeline.detail: The brief epic of the temptation in the wilderness, and a tragedy about a blind man among his enemies.

timeline.label: The twelve-book second edition; Milton dies
timeline.detail: Books VII and X were each split in two and a few lines added. Milton died in November and was buried at St Giles-without-Cripplegate.

timeline.label: Tonson's illustrated folio
timeline.detail: The first grand edition, published by subscription, which established the poem as a national monument rather than a recent book.

timeline.label: Blake begins The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
timeline.detail: The first of the Romantic readings that take Milton's Satan as the poem's real energy — a reading the poem's structure was built to resist.

timeline.label: Jane Austen born at Steventon
timeline.detail: The seventh child of a Hampshire rector, in a household that read aloud and wrote for each other.

timeline.label: First Impressions drafted
timeline.detail: Written in 1796–97, in Austen’s early twenties. No manuscript of this version survives.

timeline.label: The manuscript is offered to Thomas Cadell
timeline.detail: Austen’s father wrote to the London publisher, who declined without asking to see it. The novel waited more than a decade.

timeline.label: Sense and Sensibility published
timeline.detail: Austen’s first published novel, issued anonymously, made a second Austen title commercially plausible.

timeline.label: Pride and Prejudice published
timeline.detail: Thomas Egerton issued it in three volumes on 28 January, credited to the author of Sense and Sensibility. A second edition followed the same year.

timeline.label: Mansfield Park published
timeline.detail: The first of Austen’s novels written entirely after she had become a published author.

timeline.label: Emma published
timeline.detail: Issued by John Murray with an 1816 date on the title page.

timeline.label: Austen dies at Winchester
timeline.detail: She was forty-one. Her name had still not appeared on a title page.

timeline.label: Northanger Abbey and Persuasion published together
timeline.detail: Issued in the last days of 1817 with 1818 on the title page, and carrying the biographical notice by her brother Henry that named her at last.

timeline.label: Richard Bentley reprints the novels
timeline.detail: Austen enters the cheap standard-novel market, and stays in print from this point on.

timeline.label: The Peacock edition
timeline.detail: George Allen publishes Hugh Thomson’s illustrated edition, whose gilt peacock binding became the novel’s most recognisable object.

timeline.label: MGM’s Pride and Prejudice
timeline.detail: Directed by Robert Z. Leonard, with Greer Garson and Laurence Olivier, and costumed with cheerful disregard for the Regency.

timeline.label: BBC serial adapted by Andrew Davies
timeline.detail: Jennifer Ehle and Colin Firth in six episodes; the version against which most later screen Darcys are measured.

timeline.label: Joe Wright’s film
timeline.detail: Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen, in a version that puts mud, livestock and noise back into Longbourn.

books.title: The Tragedy of Pudd’nhead Wilson
books.author: Mark Twain
books.written: 1892-93, at Florence, out of a farce about Siamese twins that Twain cut in half

timeline.label: The novel's opening: Roxy switches the babies in 1830
timeline.detail: Roxy changes the two babies in the Driscoll nursery; both are about seven months old.

timeline.label: Clemens's boyhood in Hannibal, Missouri
timeline.detail: Hannibal, Missouri, where Samuel Clemens grew up watching slaves shipped south, is the model for Dawson's Landing.

timeline.label: The novel's murder trial, set in 1853
timeline.detail: The murder of Judge Driscoll and Wilson's finger-print demonstration close the novel's action.

timeline.label: Faulds and Herschel argue for finger-prints
timeline.detail: Letters in Nature propose using finger-prints for identification, a decade before Twain wrote the trial.

timeline.label: Galton's Finger Prints published
timeline.detail: Francis Galton's book established that the patterns are unique and unchanging; Twain read about the method while the novel was in progress.

timeline.label: Begun as a farce
timeline.detail: Twain started a comic story about conjoined twins in Florence, then found the changeling plot taking it over.

timeline.label: Twain cuts the Siamese twins out of the novel
timeline.detail: He separated the brothers, pulled their story out as Those Extraordinary Twins, and rewrote what remained.

timeline.label: Serialised in The Century
timeline.detail: The novel ran in The Century Magazine from December 1893 to June 1894, with illustrations.

timeline.label: Published as a book
timeline.detail: The American Publishing Company issued it with Those Extraordinary Twins appended and Twain's note explaining the surgery.

timeline.label: Plessy v. Ferguson
timeline.detail: Two years after publication the Supreme Court upheld segregation in a case turning on a man who was seven-eighths white.

timeline.label: Leslie Fiedler's defence
timeline.detail: Fiedler called the novel a great and neglected American book, and modern criticism of it effectively starts here.

timeline.label: The American Civil War begins
timeline.detail: The war Crane's novel is set in, and which he was born too late to see.

timeline.label: The Battle of Chancellorsville
timeline.detail: Fought in Virginia in early May: confused fighting in woodland, and a Union defeat. Long associated with the novel, though Crane never names it.

timeline.label: The war ends
timeline.detail: Veterans' reminiscences, many of them published in magazines Crane read, became a large part of American periodical writing.

timeline.label: Stephen Crane born in Newark, New Jersey
timeline.detail: The fourteenth child of a Methodist minister, and six years too late for the war he made his name on.

timeline.label: Crane's Maggie: A Girl of the Streets published
timeline.detail: Crane's first novel, printed at his own expense and largely unsold.

timeline.label: A shortened version syndicated in newspapers
timeline.detail: The story reached its first readers cut down for the press, before any publisher would take the full book.

timeline.label: Published by D. Appleton and Company
timeline.detail: The book made Crane famous in his early twenties, in Britain as well as in America.

timeline.label: Crane shipwrecked off the Florida coast
timeline.detail: The sinking of the Commodore, on a gun-running voyage to Cuba, produced 'The Open Boat'.

timeline.label: Crane reports from Cuba as a war correspondent
timeline.detail: Reporting the Spanish-American War finally gave him the experience readers had assumed lay behind the novel.

timeline.label: Crane dies at Badenweiler
timeline.detail: Of tuberculosis, in a German sanatorium, aged twenty-eight.

timeline.label: John Huston's film
timeline.detail: With Audie Murphy, one of the most decorated American soldiers of the Second World War, as Henry; the studio cut it heavily before release.

timeline.label: Richard of Bordeaux is born
timeline.detail: Son of Edward the Black Prince, and grandson of Edward III.

timeline.label: Richard becomes king as a child
timeline.detail: He succeeds his grandfather Edward III at the age of ten, his own father having died the year before.

timeline.label: The Peasants' Revolt
timeline.detail: The young king faces the rebels in person, an episode Shakespeare leaves out of a play that begins seventeen years later.

timeline.label: Bolingbroke and Mowbray are banished
timeline.detail: The quarrel with which the play opens ends in exile rather than trial by combat.

timeline.label: Gaunt dies, Bolingbroke returns, Richard is deposed
timeline.detail: The confiscation of the Lancastrian inheritance and the landing at Ravenspurgh fall in the same year as the surrender of the crown.

timeline.label: Richard dies in captivity at Pontefract
timeline.detail: The play calls the castle Pomfret and gives him a murderer; the historical cause of death is not certain.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: The second edition gave Shakespeare the sequence of events for this play and the ones that follow it.

timeline.label: The play is written
timeline.detail: Usually dated to about this year, which places it at the head of the second sequence of English histories.

timeline.label: The first quarto is printed
timeline.detail: Printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise, without the deposition passage in 4.1.

timeline.label: A Richard II play is staged before the Essex rising
timeline.detail: Supporters of the Earl of Essex paid for a performance of a play about Richard II on the eve of the revolt; the record does not name Shakespeare's text outright, but the subject was enough to make it dangerous.

timeline.label: Fourth Quarto adds the deposition scene
timeline.detail: The title page announces the Parliament scene and the deposing of King Richard as material now in print.

timeline.label: The First Folio
timeline.detail: The play is printed among the histories, fixing its place at the start of the run to Henry V.

timeline.label: Tewkesbury, and the death of Henry VI
timeline.detail: Two killings the play keeps returning to: Prince Edward at the battle and his father in the Tower.

timeline.label: Edward IV dies and Richard takes the throne
timeline.detail: The events of Acts II to IV are compressed from a few months of this year.

timeline.label: Bosworth Field
timeline.detail: Richard is killed on 22 August and Henry Tudor is crowned; Bosworth is conventionally taken as the end of the Wars of the Roses.

timeline.label: Thomas More's history of Richard III printed
timeline.detail: Written decades earlier and left unfinished, it supplied the Tudor chroniclers with the calculating, theatrical Richard Shakespeare inherited.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's immediate source, which carries More's account through Hall into the material of the play.

timeline.label: The True Tragedy of Richard the Third printed
timeline.detail: An anonymous play on the same story, evidence that Richard was already established stage material.

timeline.label: First quarto
timeline.detail: Printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise, and reprinted repeatedly over the next four decades.

timeline.label: Second quarto names Shakespeare
timeline.detail: The first of his plays to be widely reprinted in his lifetime carries his name from this edition onwards.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: A substantially different and longer text, printed among the histories.

timeline.label: Colley Cibber's adaptation
timeline.detail: A shortened rewriting that cut Margaret altogether and held the English stage for the best part of two centuries.

timeline.label: Garrick's debut as Richard
timeline.detail: The role made his name in London, and made the part an actor's proving ground.

timeline.label: Edmund Kean's Richard at Drury Lane
timeline.detail: A fast, unheroic reading that became the standard against which nineteenth-century Richards were measured.

timeline.label: Laurence Olivier's film
timeline.detail: Still using much of Cibber's shape, it fixed the opening soliloquy in the popular ear for a century of listeners.

timeline.label: Richard III's remains found in Leicester
timeline.detail: The skeleton showed severe scoliosis, reopening old arguments about how much of the play's body is Tudor invention.

timeline.label: The novel’s date for Crusoe’s birth: 1632, at York
timeline.detail: The first sentence of the novel gives the year, the city and his father’s origins in Bremen.

timeline.label: The novel’s shipwreck: 30 September 1659
timeline.detail: 30 September 1659, the date the journal opens on and the day notched at the head of the post.

timeline.label: Daniel Defoe born in London
timeline.detail: The son of a tallow chandler, educated for the Dissenting ministry and afterwards a merchant, bankrupt and pamphleteer.

timeline.label: The novel’s rescue: Crusoe leaves the island, 19 December 1686
timeline.detail: 19 December 1686, after eight-and-twenty years, two months and nineteen days.

timeline.label: Defoe pilloried for The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
timeline.detail: A satire taken for the thing it imitated — an early demonstration of how completely he could disappear into a voice.

timeline.label: Alexander Selkirk is put ashore on Juan Fernández
timeline.detail: He was taken off in 1709; his case was widely reported and is the nearest thing the novel has to a documented source.

timeline.label: Robinson Crusoe published
timeline.detail: 25 April, by William Taylor, with no author’s name and a title page promising a life written by Crusoe himself.

timeline.label: The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe published
timeline.detail: Published in August of the same year, taking Crusoe back to the island and on to China and Siberia.

timeline.label: Serious Reflections During the Life of Robinson Crusoe published
timeline.detail: A third volume of essays, in which the story is defended as an allegory of Defoe’s own life.

timeline.label: Defoe dies in Ropemaker’s Alley, London
timeline.detail: In lodgings, evading creditors, having written more than most of his contemporaries had read.

timeline.label: Rousseau makes it the one book in Émile’s library
timeline.detail: In Émile, Robinson Crusoe is recommended as the whole of a boy’s early reading — the beginning of its career as an educational text.

timeline.label: Matteo Bandello publishes his Novelle
timeline.detail: His version of the Veronese lovers carries the story into the European collections that reach England.

timeline.label: Pierre Boaistuau adapts Bandello into French
timeline.detail: The Histoires tragiques supply the immediate source for the English versions.

timeline.label: Arthur Brooke's poem Romeus and Juliet published
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's chief English source: the feud, the Friar, the Nurse, the potion and the tomb, spread across months.

timeline.label: William Painter prints a prose version
timeline.detail: The Palace of Pleasure shows how far the Italian novella tradition had entered English reading.

timeline.label: First Quarto printed by John Danter
timeline.detail: An Excellent conceited Tragedie of Romeo and Iuliet; the title page claims frequent public performance by the Lord Hunsdon's Servants.

timeline.label: Second Quarto: 'newly corrected, augmented, and amended'
timeline.detail: Much fuller than Q1, and the basis of later quartos, the Folio text and modern editions.

timeline.label: The play is entered in the Stationers' Register
timeline.detail: A decade after the first quarto had already appeared in print.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed as The Tragedie of Romeo and Juliet, following the later quarto line.

timeline.label: David Garrick's acting version
timeline.detail: Restores more of Shakespeare's text than earlier adaptations while rewriting the ending for the eighteenth-century stage.

timeline.label: Gounod's Roméo et Juliette
timeline.detail: The opera makes the love plot the musical engine and gives the lovers extended duets.

timeline.label: Prokofiev composes the ballet score
timeline.detail: It becomes the basis of the best-known dance treatments, including Kenneth MacMillan's of 1965.

timeline.label: West Side Story opens
timeline.detail: The feud is transferred to New York gang conflict, with music by Leonard Bernstein and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim.

timeline.label: Zeffirelli's film
timeline.detail: Casting Leonard Whiting and Olivia Hussey as genuinely young leads changed what audiences expected the parts to look like.

timeline.label: Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's language kept intact inside a modern Verona Beach of guns, television and religious iconography.

books.title: Sense and Sensibility
books.author: Jane Austen
books.written: Begun in the 1790s, probably as Elinor and Marianne; revised for publication by 1811

timeline.label: Jane Austen born at Steventon
timeline.detail: In the Hampshire rectory where she wrote the first versions of three of her six novels.

timeline.label: Early version, Elinor and Marianne, probably written
timeline.detail: Family tradition places an early version of this story in the mid-1790s, probably told in letters. No manuscript survives.

timeline.label: First Impressions offered to a publisher and refused
timeline.detail: The novel that became Pride and Prejudice was declined unseen, and Austen published nothing for another fourteen years.

timeline.label: The Austens settle at Chawton
timeline.detail: The move to a settled house in Hampshire begins the period in which every one of Austen’s novels was revised or written.

timeline.label: Sense and Sensibility published
timeline.detail: Printed for the author by C. Roworth, published by T. Egerton in three volumes, and advertised at fifteen shillings in boards.

timeline.label: The first edition sells out; a second follows
timeline.detail: In the same year Pride and Prejudice appeared as ‘by the author of Sense and Sensibility’, turning an anonymous debut into a commercial identity.

timeline.label: Mansfield Park published
timeline.detail: The first novel Austen wrote knowing that she had readers.

timeline.label: Austen dies at Winchester
timeline.detail: Aged forty-one, with none of her novels published under her own name.

timeline.label: Bentley’s Standard Novels reprint
timeline.detail: Sense and Sensibility re-enters the market in a cheap uniform edition, and Austen’s novels stop going out of print.

timeline.label: First BBC television adaptation
timeline.detail: The beginning of a long serial tradition that gives the social network around the sisters more room than a feature film can.

timeline.label: Ang Lee’s film, from Emma Thompson’s screenplay
timeline.detail: Thompson as Elinor, Kate Winslet as Marianne, Alan Rickman as Brandon; it won the Academy Award for Adapted Screenplay and the Golden Bear at Berlin.

timeline.label: Kandukondain Kandukondain, a Tamil film adaptation
timeline.detail: Rajiv Menon’s Tamil-language film relocates the sisters, the prospects and the delayed recognition to an Indian setting.

timeline.label: BBC serial adapted by Andrew Davies
timeline.detail: A three-part version directed by John Alexander, which restores the seduction plot to its place near the front of the story.

books.title: Shakespeare’s Sonnets
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.written: Between about 1591 and 1604, over more than a decade rather than in one campaign

timeline.label: Sidney's Astrophil and Stella printed
timeline.detail: The sonnet sequence becomes the fashionable English form almost overnight; Daniel, Drayton, Spenser and others follow within five years.

timeline.label: Venus and Adonis published
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's first printed book, dedicated to the Earl of Southampton — the period when the earliest sonnets were probably written.

timeline.label: The Rape of Lucrece published
timeline.detail: A second dedication to Southampton, warmer than the first, and the last time Shakespeare put his name to a dedication.

timeline.label: Francis Meres names the sonnets
timeline.detail: Palladis Tamia refers to sugared sonnets circulating among Shakespeare's private friends, so a substantial group existed in manuscript.

timeline.label: Sonnets 138 and 144 printed in The Passionate Pilgrim
timeline.detail: The Passionate Pilgrim prints early versions of sonnets 138 and 144 under Shakespeare's name.

timeline.label: Thomas Thorpe publishes the quarto
timeline.detail: SHAKE-SPEARES SONNETS is entered in the Stationers' Register on 20 May and published with the dedication to Mr. W.H. It was not reprinted for thirty-one years.

timeline.label: Benson's edition rearranges the poems
timeline.detail: John Benson reorders the sequence, runs poems together under invented titles and changes some pronouns from male to female.

timeline.label: Malone restores the 1609 text
timeline.detail: Edmond Malone prints the sonnets in their quarto order with numbers and notes, the basis of every later edition.

timeline.label: Steevens refuses to reprint them
timeline.detail: George Steevens leaves the sonnets out of his edition of Shakespeare, saying no act of parliament could make readers face them — the clearest record of eighteenth-century embarrassment.

timeline.label: Wilde's The Portrait of Mr. W. H.
timeline.detail: A story about the search for the young man that is also a defence of reading the poems as love poems between men.

timeline.label: The Variorum edition
timeline.detail: Hyder Rollins collects three centuries of commentary in two volumes and shows how little the biographical questions have been settled.

timeline.label: Duncan-Jones's Arden edition
timeline.detail: Katherine Duncan-Jones argues that the 1609 quarto was authorised by Shakespeare, reopening a question that had been treated as closed.

timeline.label: The Indian Rebellion
timeline.detail: Beginning among sepoys of the Bengal army in May and spreading across northern India. Europeans from the surrounding country took refuge in the fort at Agra, as Small does, and an action was fought outside the city early in July.

timeline.label: A penal settlement is founded at Port Blair
timeline.detail: The British opened the convict colony on the Andaman Islands in the aftermath of the rebellion, and many of its first prisoners were men sentenced for their part in it. Small and his three partners are sent there.

timeline.label: Arthur Conan Doyle is born in Edinburgh
timeline.detail: He studied medicine at the university there and went into general practice at Southsea in 1882.

timeline.label: Wilkie Collins publishes The Moonstone
timeline.detail: The earlier English novel of an Indian jewel looted in wartime and followed home. Collins sends the stone back; Doyle sends it to the bottom of the river.

timeline.label: A Study in Scarlet appears in Beeton’s Christmas Annual
timeline.detail: Holmes and Watson’s first case, which Holmes criticises in the opening chapter of this one. It made little stir.

timeline.label: Commissioned at a dinner at the Langham Hotel
timeline.detail: On 30 August Joseph Marshall Stoddart, over from Philadelphia for Lippincott’s, entertained Doyle and Oscar Wilde and came away with a promise of a story from each. Doyle wrote his that autumn. Wilde’s was The Picture of Dorian Gray. The Langham is where Captain Morstan vanishes.

timeline.label: Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine prints the novel complete
timeline.detail: In the February number, as The Sign of the Four; or, The Problem of the Sholtos.

timeline.label: Spencer Blackett publishes the first book edition
timeline.detail: In October, under the shorter title The Sign of Four, which many later editions keep.

timeline.label: The Holmes short stories begin in the Strand Magazine
timeline.detail: A Scandal in Bohemia appeared in July. It was the monthly stories, not the two novels, that made Holmes a public figure, and sent readers back to this book.

timeline.label: Maurice Elvey films the novel for Stoll Pictures
timeline.detail: A silent feature with Eille Norwood as Holmes, the last of his long run in the part.

timeline.label: Doyle dies at Crowborough in Sussex
timeline.detail: Knighted in 1902, and by then far better known for Holmes than for the historical novels he valued more.

timeline.label: Arthur Wontner plays Holmes in a sound film of the story
timeline.detail: Directed by Graham Cutts, with Ian Hunter as Watson; the plot is rearranged so that the Agra backstory comes first.

timeline.label: Granada Television’s feature-length adaptation
timeline.detail: Jeremy Brett as Holmes and Edward Hardwicke as Watson, directed by Peter Hammond. It drops Watson’s engagement altogether.

books.title: Sleepy Hollow and Other American Halloween Stories
books.author: Washington Irving, Edgar Allan Poe and others
books.written: Between 1820 and 1926, by seven writers who had no October holiday in mind

timeline.label: The Revolution ends
timeline.detail: The Hessian trooper of the legend is a soldier of that war, which was within living memory when Irving wrote.

timeline.label: Irving's 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow' published
timeline.detail: Published in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent., which made Irving the first American author to live by his pen abroad.

timeline.label: Irving's 'The Devil and Tom Walker' published
timeline.detail: Printed in Tales of a Traveller, moving the same comic-gothic method to New England money.

timeline.label: Hawthorne's 'Young Goodman Brown' published
timeline.detail: Hawthorne, a descendant of a Salem witch-trial judge, publishes the forest story anonymously in a magazine.

timeline.label: Poe's 'The Fall of the House of Usher' published
timeline.detail: Poe in Burton's Gentleman's Magazine, setting the terms for American gothic interiors.

timeline.label: Poe's 'The Tell-Tale Heart' and 'The Black Cat' published
timeline.detail: The Tell-Tale Heart and The Black Cat appear within months of each other.

timeline.label: Bierce's 'The Boarded Window' published
timeline.detail: Bierce, a Civil War veteran, publishes the frontier story whose last line does all the work.

timeline.label: Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 'The Yellow Wall-Paper' published
timeline.detail: Gilman's story of a rest cure appears in The New England Magazine.

timeline.label: Mary Wilkins Freeman's 'The Shadows on the Wall' published
timeline.detail: Mary Wilkins Freeman's New England ghost story, told almost entirely through the household's conversation.

timeline.label: Lovecraft's 'The Outsider' in Weird Tales
timeline.detail: Lovecraft in Weird Tales, closing the century the collection covers.

timeline.label: Gascoigne's Supposes performed at Gray's Inn
timeline.detail: An English version of Ariosto's I Suppositi, and the source of the Bianca plot's disguises and substituted fathers.

timeline.label: Supposes printed
timeline.detail: Its availability in print is what makes the borrowing traceable.

timeline.label: The Taming of the Shrew probably written
timeline.detail: Usually placed around 1590-92 among the earliest comedies; nothing fixes the year.

timeline.label: The Taming of a Shrew, a closely related play, printed
timeline.detail: A closely related play with different names and wording, reprinted in 1596 and 1607. Source, memorial report, adaptation or early draft: the question is still open.

timeline.label: Fletcher's The Woman's Prize, or The Tamer Tamed
timeline.detail: Usually dated around 1609-11. Petruchio remarries after Katherina's death and is resisted by a second wife, which shows the play was being answered within its own generation.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The first secure printed text of Shakespeare's Shrew, with the Induction and no return to Sly.

timeline.label: A quarto printed from the Folio text
timeline.detail: Not an independent witness; it confirms that the Folio was the version in circulation.

timeline.label: John Lacy's Sauny the Scot
timeline.detail: A Restoration adaptation in prose that expanded Grumio into a Scottish servant and made Petruchio harsher.

timeline.label: Garrick's Catharine and Petruchio
timeline.detail: Three acts, no Sly, almost no Bianca — and the version most audiences saw for well over a century.

timeline.label: Sam Taylor's film with Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks
timeline.detail: Widely cited as the first sound Shakespeare film; Pickford's wink during the last speech became part of the play's argument with itself.

timeline.label: Kiss Me, Kate opens on Broadway
timeline.detail: Cole Porter's musical puts the play inside a backstage quarrel — a twentieth-century replacement for the abandoned Sly frame.

timeline.label: Michael Bogdanov's RSC production
timeline.detail: Sly disrupted the auditorium before the Padua story began, treating the taming plot as a problem rather than a farce.

timeline.label: Justin Audibert's gender-reversed RSC production
timeline.detail: Set in a matriarchal Elizabethan England, with Petruchia and Katherine, so that the hierarchy itself became visible as a construction.

timeline.label: Thomas Hardy born at Higher Bockhampton
timeline.detail: In a cottage on the edge of the heath, three miles from Dorchester, into a family of builders and masons.

timeline.label: The Elementary Education Act
timeline.detail: The schooling that gives Tess her Sixth Standard English and opens the two-hundred-year gap Hardy describes between her and her mother.

timeline.label: Far from the Madding Crowd
timeline.detail: The novel that made Hardy’s name and fixed Wessex as a place readers expected to revisit.

timeline.label: The Mayor of Casterbridge
timeline.detail: Dorchester under its Wessex name, and the same interest in a man ruined by a single early act.

timeline.label: Serialised in The Graphic
timeline.detail: Weekly from July to December, with the seduction, the baptism and other material cut or altered for a family illustrated paper.

timeline.label: First book edition
timeline.detail: Three volumes from James R. Osgood, McIlvaine and Co., restoring the excised material and carrying the subtitle A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented.

timeline.label: One-volume edition
timeline.detail: A cheaper single volume widens the readership, and Hardy goes on revising the text in later issues.

timeline.label: Jude the Obscure
timeline.detail: The reception of Hardy’s last novel effectively ended his career as a novelist; he wrote poetry for the next thirty years.

timeline.label: Lorimer Stoddard’s stage version opens in New York
timeline.detail: Minnie Maddern Fiske played Tess from 2 March, and made the part a major role in the American theatre.

timeline.label: Silent film with Blanche Sweet
timeline.detail: Blanche Sweet as Tess, Stuart Holmes as Alec and Conrad Nagel as Angel; the film is now considered lost.

timeline.label: Hardy dies
timeline.detail: His ashes were buried in Westminster Abbey and his heart at Stinsford, which is the most Hardyan fact about him.

timeline.label: Roman Polanski’s Tess
timeline.detail: Nastassja Kinski in the title role; the film won Academy Awards for cinematography, art direction and costume design.

timeline.label: BBC four-part adaptation
timeline.detail: Written by David Nicholls and directed by David Blair, with Gemma Arterton as Tess.

books.title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
books.author: Mark Twain
books.written: Drafted in the early 1870s at Hartford and Quarry Farm

timeline.label: Samuel Langhorne Clemens born at Florida, Missouri
timeline.detail: The family moved to Hannibal on the Mississippi four years later.

timeline.label: The Clemens family moves to Hannibal
timeline.detail: The river town, its cave, its hill and its social order supply nearly everything St Petersburg is made of.

timeline.label: The Civil War begins
timeline.detail: The book, written afterwards, looks back at a Missouri slaveholding town and never says so directly.

timeline.label: First edition published in London
timeline.detail: Chatto & Windus issued the book on 9 June, ahead of any authorised American printing.

timeline.label: Pirated in Toronto, and published in the United States
timeline.detail: Belford Brothers’ unauthorised Canadian edition appeared on 29 July; the American Publishing Company’s illustrated edition followed in December.

timeline.label: True W. Williams illustrates the American edition
timeline.detail: His pictures shaped how the book was sold by subscription, and are discussed rather than reproduced in the Astor edition.

timeline.label: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn published in Britain
timeline.detail: The American edition followed in 1885; the sequel gives the narration to the boy Tom treats as an accessory.

timeline.label: Pudd’nhead Wilson published
timeline.detail: Twain returns to the same river town and puts slavery, identity and the law at the centre rather than the edge.

timeline.label: Mark Twain dies at Redding, Connecticut
timeline.detail: By then Tom Sawyer had long outsold its first, disappointing season.

timeline.label: The Technicolor film adaptation
timeline.detail: Produced by David O. Selznick, it fixed the fence, the cave and the funeral as the story’s three scenes for a mass audience.

timeline.label: Kate O'Flaherty born in St Louis
timeline.detail: Of Irish and French Creole descent; her father was killed in a railway accident when she was five.

timeline.label: Marriage to Oscar Chopin, and a move to New Orleans
timeline.detail: The twelve years in Louisiana gave her nearly all the material of her fiction.

timeline.label: Oscar Chopin dies
timeline.detail: Chopin ran the family business for a time and then returned to St Louis with six children.

timeline.label: At Fault, Chopin's first novel, published
timeline.detail: Published at her own expense, and little noticed.

timeline.label: The hurricane destroys Chênière Caminada
timeline.detail: The Gulf community Edna visits with Robert had been devastated a few years before the novel was written.

timeline.label: Chopin's Bayou Folk published
timeline.detail: The Louisiana stories that made her reputation as a regional writer, which is the reputation The Awakening broke.

timeline.label: Chopin begins the novel, then titled A Solitary Soul
timeline.detail: A second story collection appeared while she was at work on the book, then titled A Solitary Soul.

timeline.label: The manuscript finished
timeline.detail: Dated 21 January 1898, more than a year before it reached print.

timeline.label: Published by Herbert S. Stone & Company
timeline.detail: On 22 April, in Chicago. Reviewers treated the book as a moral question rather than a literary one.

timeline.label: Removed from Evanston Public Library
timeline.detail: A documented removal. The often-repeated claim that St Louis libraries banned the book has no evidence behind it.

timeline.label: Chopin dies in St Louis
timeline.detail: On 22 August, five years after the novel appeared and with her third story collection still unpublished.

timeline.label: Per Seyersted's biography and collected works
timeline.detail: The scholarly edition and critical study that returned the novel to print and to serious reading.

timeline.label: Punch begins publication
timeline.detail: The weekly that would print the diary in twenty-six instalments, read largely by the professional and clerical households it made its subject.

timeline.label: George Grossmith is born in London
timeline.detail: On 9 December, son of a police-court reporter. He worked at Bow Street himself before making a living on the platform as a comic singer at the piano.

timeline.label: Weedon Grossmith is born in London
timeline.detail: On 9 June. He trained as a painter and exhibited before turning to the stage, and is credited as co-author of the book as well as its illustrator.

timeline.label: George Grossmith joins the Gilbert and Sullivan company
timeline.detail: He created John Wellington Wells in The Sorcerer and went on to the run of leading comic parts, among them Sir Joseph Porter, Bunthorne, the Lord Chancellor and Ko-Ko.

timeline.label: The Cheap Trains Act
timeline.detail: Railway companies are obliged to run workmen's trains at low fares, one of the pressures that turned districts such as Holloway into streets of small rented villas — with, as at The Laurels, the line at the end of the garden and two pounds off the rent.

timeline.label: The 'Is Marriage a Failure?' press correspondence
timeline.detail: Set off by Mona Caird's article on marriage in the Westminster Review that August and carried on at length in the daily press. Pooter and Carrie talk it over on 2 November and agree that it has been no failure in their case.

timeline.label: The serial begins in Punch
timeline.detail: Twenty-six instalments between May 1888 and May 1889, written by George Grossmith while he was still playing nightly for D'Oyly Carte.

timeline.label: George Grossmith leaves the D'Oyly Carte company
timeline.detail: After twelve years of comic leads he returned to touring as a solo entertainer, which had been his living before Gilbert and Sullivan and remained more profitable.

timeline.label: The Eiffel Tower opens in Paris
timeline.detail: Named by Hardfur Huttle at Franching's dinner, beside the Brooklyn Bridge, as the kind of thing a man of the happy medium will never build.

timeline.label: J. W. Arrowsmith publishes the book in Bristol
timeline.detail: Expanded by roughly four months of entries and illustrated with twenty-six drawings by Weedon Grossmith. The same firm had published Three Men in a Boat three years earlier.

timeline.label: A new issue carries prefatory tributes
timeline.detail: The early book editions attracted little notice; the 1910 issue, with appreciations by Lord Rosebery and Augustine Birrell, marks the point at which the book's standing was made by admirers rather than by sales.

timeline.label: George Grossmith dies at Folkestone
timeline.detail: On 1 March. He had published two volumes of reminiscence of his own, which is one of the jokes behind Pooter's preface.

timeline.label: Weedon Grossmith dies
timeline.detail: On 14 June, after a second career as actor, playwright and theatre manager, and a memoir of his own about the move from painting to the stage.

timeline.label: Ken Russell films the diary for the BBC
timeline.detail: Made for the arts programme Monitor and played as a silent comedy with captions, which suits a book whose narrator cannot hear how he sounds.

timeline.label: A four-part adaptation on BBC Four
timeline.detail: With Hugh Bonneville as Pooter speaking the entries straight to camera, the nearest television has come to reproducing the effect of the diary form.

timeline.label: Giovanna d'Aragona widowed, c. 1498
timeline.detail: Her husband, Alfonso Piccolomini, Duke of Amalfi, died, and she governed the duchy for their son. Her brother Luigi was a cardinal.

timeline.label: The play's own date: Bosola's horoscope reads 1504
timeline.detail: The nativity Bosola picks up in 2.3 is dated 1504, which places the action, loosely, in the first years of the sixteenth century.

timeline.label: Antonio Bologna killed in Milan, c. 1513
timeline.detail: The historical Antonio Beccadelli di Bologna was murdered after the Duchess and their children had disappeared. Bandello, who says he knew him, names the leader of the killers as Daniele da Bozolo, the source of Bosola's name.

timeline.label: Bandello's novellas printed
timeline.detail: The Duchess's story appears in the first part of Matteo Bandello's collection of tales, published at Lucca.

timeline.label: The Palace of Pleasure, second volume
timeline.detail: William Painter's English version of the story, taken from a French adaptation of Bandello, is the one Webster followed most closely.

timeline.label: John Webster born, c. 1580
timeline.detail: The son of a London coachmaker. Almost nothing is known of his life, and the date is an inference.

timeline.label: Galileo's telescope
timeline.detail: Galileo published his observations of the moon this year. The Cardinal's reference in 2.4 to 'that fantastic glass Invented by Galileo the Florentine' places the play after it.

timeline.label: Arbella Stuart's secret marriage
timeline.detail: A cousin of James I married William Seymour without the king's leave and was imprisoned; she died in the Tower in 1615. Her case has often been set beside the Duchess's.

timeline.label: The White Devil printed
timeline.detail: Webster's first surviving tragedy of his own, another Italian story centred on a defiant woman, came out after a winter performance that he blamed for its poor reception.

timeline.label: Performed by December, when William Ostler, the first Antonio, dies
timeline.detail: William Ostler, named as Antonio in the 1623 cast list, died in December 1614, so the play had been performed by then.

timeline.label: The first quarto
timeline.detail: Printed by Nicholas Okes for John Waterson, with commendatory verses and a list of actors that covers two different casts.

timeline.label: Ashcroft and Gielgud at the Haymarket
timeline.detail: A London revival with Peggy Ashcroft as the Duchess and John Gielgud as Ferdinand, in the last months of the Second World War.

timeline.label: Chosen to open the new Sam Wanamaker Playhouse
timeline.detail: The candlelit indoor theatre at Shakespeare's Globe, modelled on playhouses of the Blackfriars kind, opened its first season with this play.

timeline.label: F. Scott Fitzgerald born in Saint Paul, Minnesota
timeline.detail: Named for a distant relative who wrote the words of The Star-Spangled Banner.

timeline.label: Fitzgerald meets Zelda Sayre while stationed in Alabama
timeline.detail: The courtship, the refusal and the eventual acceptance after his first novel sold all feed the Louisville chapters.

timeline.label: The World Series is fixed
timeline.detail: The scandal that gives Meyer Wolfshiem his introduction in Chapter 4, and dates the world Gatsby's money comes from.

timeline.label: National prohibition takes effect, and This Side of Paradise is published
timeline.detail: The law that creates Gatsby's business and the book that made his author famous arrive in the same year.

timeline.label: The summer of 1922, in which the novel is set
timeline.detail: Fitzgerald was living at Great Neck on Long Island and beginning to plan a third novel.

timeline.label: The main draft is written in France
timeline.detail: A pencil manuscript of more than two hundred and fifty pages, then galleys revised so heavily in Rome that whole chapters changed shape.

timeline.label: The Great Gatsby is published on 10 April
timeline.detail: Charles Scribner's Sons, New York. The reviews were mixed and the sales well short of Fitzgerald's hopes.

timeline.label: Fitzgerald dies in Hollywood
timeline.detail: He was forty-four, at work on a novel about the film industry, and his reputation was at its lowest.

timeline.label: The Armed Services Editions distribute 155,000 copies
timeline.detail: A free paperback for service personnel put the novel into more hands in a year than it had reached in twenty.

timeline.label: Works published in 1925 enter the United States public domain
timeline.detail: The first-edition text became freely available for independent editions on 1 January.

books.title: The House on the Borderland
books.author: William Hope Hodgson
books.written: 1907, in the burst of work that followed Hodgson's years at sea

timeline.label: Hodgson born in Essex
timeline.detail: The son of an Anglican clergyman who moved the family thirteen times; two of his brothers died young.

timeline.label: Hodgson goes to sea as an apprentice
timeline.detail: Apprenticed at thirteen after a first attempt to run away; eight years at sea gave him the horror of the ocean that runs through all his work.

timeline.label: Hodgson opens a gymnasium in Blackburn
timeline.detail: He left the sea, opened a gymnasium in Blackburn and photographed storms; the discipline shows in his fiction's practicality.

timeline.label: Hodgson's first novel, The Boats of the Glen Carrig
timeline.detail: His first novel, published the year this one was written.

timeline.label: Author's introduction dated 17 December 1907
timeline.detail: The author's introduction is signed December 17, 1907.

timeline.label: Published by Chapman & Hall
timeline.detail: Reviewers admired the siege and were baffled by the cosmic chapters.

timeline.label: Hodgson's The Night Land published
timeline.detail: His last and longest novel takes the end-of-the-sun material of this book and builds a whole world on it.

timeline.label: Hodgson killed at Ypres
timeline.detail: He enlisted at thirty-seven, was invalided out, re-enlisted, and was killed by a shell in April 1918.

timeline.label: Lovecraft praises the novel in Supernatural Horror in Literature
timeline.detail: Supernatural Horror in Literature calls the novel's cosmic sweep a classic of the first water and begins its rescue.

timeline.label: Arkham House reprint
timeline.detail: The House on the Borderland and Other Novels put Hodgson back in print in America and fixed his reputation.

books.title: The Iliad
books.author: Homer
books.written: Composed in Greek, probably in the second half of the eighth century BCE; Samuel Butler's English prose translation appeared in 1898

timeline.label: The traditional date for the fall of Troy
timeline.detail: Calculated centuries later by the Greek scholar Eratosthenes from the genealogies of legend. It is not a record, though it falls close to a destruction that archaeologists date to around 1180 BCE at Hisarlik. The poem foresees the fall and never narrates it.

timeline.label: The Iliad takes something like its present form
timeline.detail: A scholarly estimate: probably the second half of the eighth century BCE, perhaps a little later, and probably somewhat before the Odyssey. It grew out of generations of sung poetry about the war.

timeline.label: Alexander the Great at Troy
timeline.detail: Crossing into Asia, Alexander is said by his ancient biographers to have sacrificed at Ilium and honoured the tomb of Achilles, and to have carried a copy of the Iliad on campaign.

timeline.label: Virgil dies, leaving the Aeneid
timeline.detail: The second half of Rome's epic replays the Iliad in Italy, with a Trojan now in the invader's role and a local prince, Turnus, dying at the end as Hector did.

timeline.label: Homer printed for the first time
timeline.detail: The first printed edition of the Greek text of both epics appeared in Florence, edited by Demetrius Chalcondyles.

timeline.label: Chapman's Iliad completed
timeline.detail: George Chapman published seven books of the Iliad in 1598 and the whole poem in English verse around 1611. It is the translation Keats would read two centuries later.

timeline.label: Pope's Iliad completed
timeline.detail: Alexander Pope's version in heroic couplets appeared in six volumes from 1715 and made his fortune. For a century it was the Iliad most English readers knew.

timeline.label: Keats's sonnet on Chapman's Homer
timeline.detail: 'On First Looking into Chapman's Homer', written in October 1816, compares first reading Homer in Chapman's English to sighting a new planet or an unknown ocean.

timeline.label: Samuel Butler, translator of this edition, born
timeline.detail: The translator was born at Langar in Nottinghamshire, a clergyman's son. Before he turned to Homer he farmed sheep in New Zealand, painted, wrote the satire Erewhon and argued in print against Darwin's account of evolution.

timeline.label: Schliemann digs at Hisarlik
timeline.detail: Heinrich Schliemann began large-scale excavation of the mound that Frank Calvert, who owned part of it, had already identified as Troy. The site holds many cities one above another, and which of them, if any, is Homer's is still argued.

timeline.label: Butler's prose Iliad published
timeline.detail: Rendered, as the title page says, 'for the use of those who cannot read the original', in the plain prose of Butler's own day. His Odyssey followed in 1900, and he died in 1902.

timeline.label: Scholars link Hittite Wilusa with Troy
timeline.detail: In the mid-1920s scholars reading Hittite diplomatic texts proposed that Wilusa, a kingdom in western Anatolia, was Homer's Ilios, and that its ruler Alaksandu bore the name Alexandros — Paris's other name. The identification is widely accepted; what it proves about a Trojan war is not.

timeline.label: Milman Parry's study of the Homeric epithet
timeline.detail: Parry showed that phrases like 'Hector tamer of horses' form a system fitted to the metre, of the kind a poet composing aloud would need. Fieldwork among singers in Yugoslavia in the 1930s supported the case that Homeric verse grew out of oral performance.

timeline.label: Oscar Wilde born in Dublin
timeline.detail: Educated at Trinity College Dublin and Magdalen College, Oxford.

timeline.label: The Picture of Dorian Gray published in book form
timeline.detail: Expanded from the magazine version of the previous year, with a preface answering its critics.

timeline.label: Lady Windermere's Fan opens at the St James's Theatre
timeline.detail: The first of the society comedies, and the play the title page of the 1899 Earnest uses to identify its author.

timeline.label: A Woman of No Importance opens
timeline.detail: The second society comedy, at the Haymarket.

timeline.label: Earnest written, largely at Worthing
timeline.detail: Wilde took a house on the Sussex coast with his family for the late summer; the hero's surname comes from the town.

timeline.label: An Ideal Husband opens in January
timeline.detail: For a few weeks in early 1895 Wilde had two plays running in the West End at once.

timeline.label: First performance, 14 February
timeline.detail: At the St James's Theatre, with George Alexander as Jack; the run ended within months when Wilde was tried and imprisoned.

timeline.label: Wilde released from Reading Gaol
timeline.detail: He left England for France and never returned.

timeline.label: First book edition, Leonard Smithers
timeline.detail: The three-act text corrected by Wilde, in a small issue of numbered and signed copies.

timeline.label: Wilde dies in Paris
timeline.detail: Three years after his release, and before the play had returned to the London stage under his name.

timeline.label: Anthony Asquith's film released
timeline.detail: With Edith Evans as Lady Bracknell, whose reading of the hand-bag line has shaped every performance since.

books.title: The Man Who Was Thursday
books.author: G. K. Chesterton
books.written: 1907, in the year between Heretics and Orthodoxy

timeline.label: Chesterton born in Kensington
timeline.detail: Into the comfortable London he would spend his career defending against people who found it boring.

timeline.label: Chesterton at the Slade School of Art
timeline.detail: At art school he went through the crisis of doubt and solipsism he later said the novel was written about.

timeline.label: Chesterton marries Frances Blogg
timeline.detail: The dedicatory poem to E. C. Bentley describes the period the book looks back on as ended by marriage and a creed.

timeline.label: Chesterton's first novel, The Napoleon of Notting Hill
timeline.detail: His first novel, and the first use of London suburbs as the setting for a fable about order.

timeline.label: Chesterton publishes Heretics
timeline.detail: The argument with the fashionable pessimists that the novel dramatises three years later.

timeline.label: The Man Who Was Thursday published
timeline.detail: Issued by J. W. Arrowsmith with the subtitle A Nightmare; Orthodoxy followed in the same year.

timeline.label: Chesterton received into the Catholic Church
timeline.detail: Fourteen years after the novel readers most often take as a statement of his faith.

timeline.label: First stage adaptation produced in London
timeline.detail: Mrs Cecil Chesterton and Ralph Neale's adaptation was produced in London, and the book's afterlife as a performance piece began.

timeline.label: Chesterton dies; his Autobiography published
timeline.detail: The Autobiography, published that year, insists the book was a nightmare about the doubt of the eighteen-nineties rather than a theological statement.

timeline.label: Orson Welles's Mercury Theatre radio adaptation
timeline.detail: The Mercury Theatre on the Air adapted the novel for radio in September, two months before the War of the Worlds broadcast.

timeline.label: Il Pecorone reaches print
timeline.detail: Ser Giovanni Fiorentino's fourteenth-century collection contains the bond, the trial and the lady disguised as a lawyer.

timeline.label: Roderigo Lopez is executed in London
timeline.detail: The queen's Portuguese physician, of Jewish descent, was convicted of conspiracy; the trial fed a wave of public feeling in the years just before the play.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register
timeline.detail: Registered to James Roberts as the Merchant of Venice, two years before it was printed.

timeline.label: First Quarto
timeline.detail: The earliest printed text, and the basis of most modern editions.

timeline.label: First recorded performance, at court
timeline.detail: The first recorded performance, on 10 February, with a repeat before the court two days later.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies, following the quarto text closely.

timeline.label: Charles Macklin plays Shylock at Drury Lane
timeline.detail: He abandoned the comic red wig of the Restoration stage and played the part seriously, which changed the play's reputation.

timeline.label: Edmund Kean's London debut as Shylock
timeline.detail: A performance that made the moneylender a figure of tragic force rather than a stage villain.

timeline.label: Henry Irving's Shylock at the Lyceum
timeline.detail: Irving's dignified, sympathetic reading dominated the late Victorian stage and shaped expectations for decades.

timeline.label: Michael Radford's film
timeline.detail: A screen version set in a carefully reconstructed Venice, with Al Pacino as Shylock and an opening sequence about the ghetto.

timeline.label: The storming of Seringapatam
timeline.detail: British forces take the city in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War; Collins places the theft of the diamond in the confusion of the assault.

timeline.label: Wilkie Collins born in London
timeline.detail: The son of the landscape painter William Collins, and later trained for the law at Lincoln’s Inn.

timeline.label: Collins meets Charles Dickens
timeline.detail: The beginning of a collaboration and a friendship that gave Collins his serial platforms.

timeline.label: The Woman in White begins in All the Year Round
timeline.detail: Collins’s first great multiple-narrator novel, and the commercial proof of the method used again here.

timeline.label: The Moonstone serialised
timeline.detail: Thirty-two weekly instalments from 4 January to 8 August, in All the Year Round and in Harper’s Weekly.

timeline.label: Three-volume edition published
timeline.detail: Tinsley Brothers issue the London book in July, before the weekly serial has finished.

timeline.label: Revised one-volume text
timeline.detail: Smith, Elder issue a revised text with a new preface for a different market and format.

timeline.label: Collins’s own dramatisation staged
timeline.detail: He adapted the novel for the theatre himself, cutting the many-narrator structure the book was built on.

timeline.label: Collins dies in London
timeline.detail: He had used laudanum for years against the pain of rheumatic illness, as Ezra Jennings does in the novel.

timeline.label: First sound film version
timeline.detail: One of a long line of adaptations that keep the theft and drop most of the narrators.

timeline.label: BBC television serial
timeline.detail: The first of several British television versions to attempt the novel’s sequence of witnesses.

books.title: The Odyssey
books.author: Homer
books.written: Composed in Greek, probably in the late eighth or early seventh century BCE; Samuel Butler's English prose translation appeared in 1900

timeline.label: The traditional date for the fall of Troy
timeline.detail: Worked out by the Greek scholar Eratosthenes centuries later. It is a calculation from legend, not a record, but it falls close to a destruction that archaeologists date to around 1180 BCE at the site of Hisarlik.

timeline.label: The Odyssey takes something like its present form
timeline.detail: Probably in the late eighth or early seventh century BCE, a little after the Iliad, in the Greek-speaking eastern Aegean. It draws on generations of oral song about the returns of the heroes from Troy.

timeline.label: Alexandrian scholars edit the text
timeline.detail: Over the third and second centuries BCE the librarians at Alexandria, Aristarchus the most influential among them, compared manuscripts and marked suspect lines. The division into twenty-four books is usually credited to this period.

timeline.label: Virgil dies, leaving the Aeneid
timeline.detail: Rome's national epic rewrites Homer: its first six books answer the Odyssey with a hero who sails west from Troy and visits the dead.

timeline.label: Homer printed for the first time
timeline.detail: The first printed edition of the Greek text of both epics appeared in Florence, edited by Demetrius Chalcondyles.

timeline.label: George Chapman's complete Homer
timeline.detail: Chapman's English Odyssey, in rhymed pentameter, had appeared about two years earlier; the collected Whole Works of Homer made both poems available to English readers without Greek.

timeline.label: Pope's Odyssey completed
timeline.detail: Alexander Pope's version in heroic couplets, produced with two collaborators, followed his Iliad and was the standard English Homer for a century.

timeline.label: Samuel Butler, the translator, born
timeline.detail: The translator was born at Langar in Nottinghamshire, a clergyman's son. He would be a sheep farmer in New Zealand, a painter, a satirist and a critic of Darwin before he turned to Homer.

timeline.label: Tennyson publishes 'Ulysses'
timeline.detail: A dramatic monologue for the hero in old age, restless in Ithaca and ready to sail again. It takes its cue from Tiresias's prophecy and from Dante rather than from Homer's ending.

timeline.label: Butler publishes The Authoress of the Odyssey
timeline.detail: Butler argued that the poem was written by a young woman in Sicily, at Trapani, who put herself into it as Nausicaa. Scholars have not accepted the theory, but it made him read the poem's domestic detail more closely than most.

timeline.label: Butler's prose Odyssey published
timeline.detail: He wanted, he said, a version for readers who knew no Greek, in the plain English of his own day. His Iliad had appeared two years before. Butler died in 1902.

timeline.label: James Joyce's Ulysses
timeline.detail: Joyce maps the Odyssey's episodes on to one day in Dublin, with an advertising canvasser as Odysseus. The Roman form of the name, as in Butler, was still the ordinary English one.

timeline.label: Milman Parry's study of the Homeric epithet
timeline.detail: Parry showed that the repeated phrases form a system fitted to the metre, of the kind a poet composing aloud would need. Fieldwork among singers in Yugoslavia in the 1930s supported the case that Homeric verse grew out of oral performance.

timeline.label: A Mycenaean palace found near Pylos
timeline.detail: Carl Blegen's excavation at Ano Englianos uncovered a Bronze Age palace and an archive of clay tablets. When their script, Linear B, was deciphered in 1952, it proved to be an early form of Greek.

timeline.label: Niccolò Machiavelli is born in Florence
timeline.detail: On 3 May, in the year Lorenzo the Magnificent took charge of the city.

timeline.label: Charles VIII of France invades Italy
timeline.detail: The Medici are driven from Florence and the republic is restored; chapter 12 dates Italy’s ruin from this unopposed march.

timeline.label: Savonarola is executed; Machiavelli enters the chancery
timeline.detail: The friar was hanged and burned in May, and within weeks Machiavelli was secretary to the Second Chancery of the republic.

timeline.label: Machiavelli is sent as envoy to Cesare Borgia
timeline.detail: He was with the duke’s court during the pacification of the Romagna and the killings at Sinigalia on the last day of the year.

timeline.label: Alexander VI dies and Julius II is elected
timeline.detail: Machiavelli was in Rome for the conclave; the conversation with Borgia reported in chapter 7 belongs to these weeks.

timeline.label: Machiavelli dismissed as the Medici return to Florence
timeline.detail: A Spanish army restored them, the republic fell, and Machiavelli was dismissed from every office he held.

timeline.label: Written on his farm after prison and release
timeline.detail: Arrested in February on suspicion of conspiracy, tortured and freed in an amnesty, he withdrew to his farm at Sant’Andrea in Percussina. A letter of 10 December to Francesco Vettori says he has written a small work on principalities.

timeline.label: Giuliano de’ Medici, the intended dedicatee, dies
timeline.detail: The letter to Vettori names Giuliano as the intended recipient; the dedication as it stands is to his nephew Lorenzo di Piero.

timeline.label: Machiavelli dies in Florence
timeline.detail: On 21 June, weeks after the Sack of Rome and the second expulsion of the Medici; the restored republic had not given him back his post.

timeline.label: First printed editions
timeline.detail: Antonio Blado printed the book in Rome, with papal privilege, and Bernardo Giunta in Florence in the same year.

timeline.label: Placed on the Roman Index of Prohibited Books
timeline.detail: All of Machiavelli’s works were banned, which did more to spread the name than the reading of him.

timeline.label: Innocent Gentillet publishes his attack on Machiavelli
timeline.detail: The French treatise commonly called the Contre-Machiavel gave northern Europe a Machiavelli made of extracted maxims, and the stage villain followed.

timeline.label: Edward Dacres’s English translation is printed
timeline.detail: The first English version to reach print, a century after English writers had begun using the name as an insult; Marriott quotes Dacres’s rendering of Petrarch at the end of chapter 26.

timeline.label: Frederick of Prussia’s Anti-Machiavel appears
timeline.detail: A refutation by a crown prince who, as king, invaded Silesia within the year.

books.title: The Railway Children
books.author: E. Nesbit
books.written: c. 1904–05, while Nesbit was living at Well Hall in Eltham, then in Kent

timeline.label: Edith Nesbit born in London
timeline.detail: The daughter of an agricultural chemist who died when she was three; the family moved often afterwards, in England and on the Continent.

timeline.label: The family settles at Halstead in Kent
timeline.detail: For about three years, in a house beside the railway. Nesbit wrote warmly about the place in later life, and it is usually identified as a model for the country of this novel, though nothing in the book names a county.

timeline.label: Marriage to Hubert Bland
timeline.detail: Their son Paul, born the same year, is the boy to whom The Railway Children is dedicated for his knowledge of railways.

timeline.label: The Fabian Society is founded
timeline.detail: Bland was a founder member and its first treasurer, and Nesbit wrote and spoke for it. The politics of this novel — a writer jailed for a book about the poor, a signalman worked past exhaustion — belong to that household.

timeline.label: The Dreyfus case begins in France
timeline.detail: A French officer convicted of passing secrets to a foreign power on documents that were not his; the verdict was finally quashed in 1906. The parallel with the father’s case is close, and there is no evidence that Nesbit had any particular trial in mind.

timeline.label: The Story of the Treasure Seekers, and the move to Well Hall
timeline.detail: Her first great success with the Bastable children, and the move to the moated house at Eltham, then in Kent, where she lived for more than twenty years and where this novel was written.

timeline.label: The Russo-Japanese War
timeline.detail: Fought from February 1904 to September 1905. It is the war the Russian exile deserts from, and the reason Perks has taken the Japanese side by the time the children meet him.

timeline.label: Serialisation in The London Magazine
timeline.detail: Thirteen monthly instalments from January 1905, which is why the chapters are so nearly self-contained. The watches the children are given are engraved with the year 1905, the only date the story puts on itself.

timeline.label: Published as a book
timeline.detail: By Wells Gardner, Darton and Co., with twenty black-and-white plates by C. E. Brock, including the frontispiece.

timeline.label: Nesbit dies in Kent
timeline.detail: At New Romney, having published some forty books for children as well as poetry, novels and ghost stories for adults.

timeline.label: A BBC television serial
timeline.detail: The last of several BBC versions, with Jenny Agutter as Bobbie; it was made in the studio and largely without trains.

timeline.label: Lionel Jeffries’s film
timeline.detail: Filmed on the Keighley and Worth Valley Railway in West Yorkshire, with Oakworth as the station, Jenny Agutter again as Bobbie and Bernard Cribbins as Perks. It fixed a Yorkshire setting on a book that never names one.

timeline.label: A television film for ITV
timeline.detail: Made on the Bluebell Railway in Sussex, with Jenny Agutter now playing the mother.

timeline.label: The Railway Children Return
timeline.detail: A sequel set among evacuees in 1944, bringing back Agutter as Bobbie and returning to Oakworth; evidence of how firmly the film’s Yorkshire has attached itself to the story.

books.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
books.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
books.written: Planned on a walk in November 1797 and finished by March 1798; revised at intervals until 1834

timeline.label: George Shelvocke's A Voyage Round the World published
timeline.detail: Its account of a rough passage round Cape Horn includes an officer shooting a black albatross in the hope of better weather. Wordsworth later recalled suggesting the incident to Coleridge.

timeline.label: Samuel Taylor Coleridge born at Ottery St Mary, Devon
timeline.detail: The youngest child of the vicar and schoolmaster of the town; he was sent to school at Christ's Hospital in London after his father's death.

timeline.label: Cook's Resolution crosses the Antarctic Circle
timeline.detail: The expedition's astronomer, William Wales, afterwards taught mathematics at Christ's Hospital while Coleridge was a pupil there, a possible route by which descriptions of polar ice reached the poem.

timeline.label: The poem is planned on a November walk in Somerset
timeline.detail: Coleridge, living at Nether Stowey, set out with William and Dorothy Wordsworth from Alfoxden towards the coast. A joint ballad was proposed to pay for the trip, and soon became Coleridge's alone.

timeline.label: Finished in March and published in Lyrical Ballads
timeline.detail: The anonymous volume, printed in Bristol, opened with 'The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere' in deliberately antique spelling, prefaced by a short prose Argument.

timeline.label: Revised for the second edition of Lyrical Ballads
timeline.detail: The spelling was modernised, the title shortened, the poem moved from the front of the volume, and Wordsworth added a note listing what he took to be its defects alongside its merits.

timeline.label: Coleridge moves to Highgate
timeline.detail: He went to live in the household of the surgeon James Gillman, seeking help with his dependence on opium, and stayed for the rest of his life.

timeline.label: Sibylline Leaves adds the marginal gloss
timeline.detail: The poem appeared under Coleridge's name for the first time, with a Latin epigraph from Thomas Burnet and a prose commentary in the margin. Biographia Literaria, with his retrospective account of the Lyrical Ballads plan, came out the same year.

timeline.label: Frankenstein quotes the poem
timeline.detail: Mary Shelley's novel gives Walton an allusion to the albatross and has Victor recite the stanza of the lonesome road, an early sign of the poem's hold on the Gothic imagination.

timeline.label: Final lifetime text; Coleridge dies at Highgate
timeline.detail: The last collected Poetical Works he oversaw prints the version now standard. He died on 25 July.

timeline.label: Gustave Doré's illustrated edition
timeline.detail: Doré's large engravings of the ice, the becalmed ship and the spectre-bark fixed the poem's look for generations of readers.

timeline.label: The novel's opening scene, set about 1642
timeline.detail: The novel places Pearl's birth in the early 1640s, some fifteen or twenty years after the settlement of Boston.

timeline.label: Governor John Winthrop dies
timeline.detail: The historical death the novel puts on the night of Dimmesdale's midnight vigil, with a meteor over the town.

timeline.label: The Salem witch trials
timeline.detail: John Hathorne sat as one of the examining magistrates; the novelist added a w to the family name.

timeline.label: Nathaniel Hawthorne born in Salem
timeline.detail: His father, a ship's captain, died in Surinam four years later.

timeline.label: Hawthorne's Twice-Told Tales published
timeline.detail: The collection that made his name among writers, if not yet among book-buyers.

timeline.label: Hawthorne is appointed Surveyor of the Port of Salem
timeline.detail: Three years in the custom house gave him the material for the book's introductory sketch.

timeline.label: Hawthorne loses his custom-house post, and his mother dies
timeline.detail: The dismissal followed a change of administration; the romance was written in the months after both events.

timeline.label: The Scarlet Letter is published in Boston
timeline.detail: Ticknor, Reed and Fields issued it in March; it sold out quickly enough to need a second printing at once.

timeline.label: Second edition, with Hawthorne's new preface
timeline.detail: Salem had taken 'The Customhouse' personally, and Hawthorne declined to withdraw a word of it.

timeline.label: Hawthorne's The House of the Seven Gables published
timeline.detail: Written in the Berkshires, where Melville was his neighbour and about to dedicate Moby-Dick to him.

timeline.label: Hawthorne dies at Plymouth, New Hampshire
timeline.detail: He was buried at Sleepy Hollow Cemetery in Concord, Massachusetts.

timeline.label: Victor Sjöström films the novel with Lillian Gish as Hester
timeline.detail: The silent version fixed a popular image of the story that stayed in circulation for decades.

timeline.label: Florio's translation of Montaigne published
timeline.detail: The English 'Of the Cannibals' behind Gonzalo's commonwealth speech becomes available.

timeline.label: The Sea Venture wrecked on Bermuda
timeline.detail: Bound for Virginia, the ship broke up on the reefs; the survivors reached Jamestown the following year.

timeline.label: Jourdain's A Discovery of the Barmudas printed
timeline.detail: One of the pamphlets that turned the wreck into a London story of storm, survival and abundant islands.

timeline.label: Performed before James I at Whitehall on 1 November
timeline.detail: The Revels record is the earliest firm evidence that the play existed and was being acted.

timeline.label: Played at court during the festivities for Princess Elizabeth's marriage
timeline.detail: One of a group of plays given by the King's Men that winter for the betrothal and wedding celebrations.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, and the volume opens with it — unusually well printed, with full stage directions and a cast list.

timeline.label: Dryden and Davenant's The Enchanted Island
timeline.detail: A Restoration rewriting that gave Miranda a sister and Caliban a mate, and held the stage for well over a century.

timeline.label: Peter Brook directs John Gielgud as Prospero
timeline.detail: At the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre; remembered for a Prospero of severity rather than serenity.

timeline.label: Jonathan Miller's colonial production
timeline.detail: Casting made the island's politics explicit, and helped establish a reading British theatre has not since put down.

timeline.label: Peter Greenaway's Prospero's Books
timeline.detail: A film that takes the library rather than the island as the centre of the play.

timeline.label: Julie Taymor's film, with Helen Mirren as Prospera
timeline.detail: Changing the magician's sex reorganises the play's questions about parenthood, exile and authority.

timeline.label: Henry James born in New York
timeline.detail: Into a family that moved repeatedly between America and Europe throughout his childhood.

timeline.label: James settles in London
timeline.detail: He spent most of the rest of his life in England and became a British subject in 1915.

timeline.label: Guy Domville fails at the St James's Theatre
timeline.detail: James was booed at his own curtain call and abandoned writing for the stage; the fiction of the following years is markedly more compressed and dramatic.

timeline.label: What Maisie Knew published
timeline.detail: Another book built on a child's partial understanding of adults, written immediately before this one.

timeline.label: Serialised in Collier's Weekly
timeline.detail: The story reached its first readers in a popular illustrated weekly rather than a literary quarterly.

timeline.label: Collected in The Two Magics
timeline.detail: Published with Covering End, so that the ghost story shared a volume with a comedy.

timeline.label: Revised for the New York Edition
timeline.detail: James reworked the text and added a preface discussing how the story was made.

timeline.label: James dies in London
timeline.detail: He had taken British nationality the previous year, during the war.

timeline.label: Britten's opera premieres in Venice
timeline.detail: The Turn of the Screw set for chamber orchestra, with Quint written for a tenor who sings, which the novella's Quint never does.

timeline.label: Jack Clayton's film The Innocents
timeline.detail: Jack Clayton's film, with Deborah Kerr as the governess and a screenplay that keeps the ambiguity deliberately open.

books.title: The Wendigo
books.author: Algernon Blackwood
books.written: Out of Blackwood's years in Canada in the 1890s, and written in the run of tales that followed The Willows

timeline.label: Blackwood born in Kent
timeline.detail: Into the evangelical household whose certainties his supernatural fiction keeps testing.
