timeline.label: Blackwood emigrates to Canada
timeline.detail: He emigrated at twenty, failed at dairy farming and hotel-keeping near Toronto, and learned the bush he writes about here.

timeline.label: Blackwood a struggling reporter in New York
timeline.detail: Years as a reporter and model, often destitute; the wilderness in his fiction is remembered from real weeks of it.

timeline.label: Blackwood returns to England
timeline.detail: He returned at thirty and began writing the stories that used the country he had left.

timeline.label: Blackwood's The Willows published
timeline.detail: The Danube story that made his reputation and set the pattern this one follows.

timeline.label: The Wendigo published
timeline.detail: In The Lost Valley and Other Stories, the collection that consolidated the reputation.

timeline.label: Lovecraft praises Blackwood in Supernatural Horror in Literature
timeline.detail: Supernatural Horror in Literature praises Blackwood above all his contemporaries and singles out the Canadian tales.

timeline.label: Blackwood begins broadcasting his stories on the BBC
timeline.detail: Blackwood began broadcasting his stories and became one of the first voices people knew from the wireless.

timeline.label: Algernon Blackwood dies
timeline.detail: He died at eighty-two, with the Canadian stories still the work most anthologised.

books.title: The Willows
books.author: Algernon Blackwood
books.written: Out of a canoe journey Blackwood made down the Danube in the summer of 1900

timeline.label: Blackwood born in Kent
timeline.detail: Into a strictly evangelical household he spent his adult life reacting against.

timeline.label: Blackwood's years in Canada and New York
timeline.detail: Farming, hotel-keeping, and years of poverty and reporting that gave him the wilderness settings of his best work.

timeline.label: Blackwood canoes down the Danube
timeline.detail: Blackwood canoed down the river through the marshes below Vienna, the trip this story is built from.

timeline.label: The Empty House, Blackwood's first collection, published
timeline.detail: His first collection appears; he is thirty-seven and writing full time.

timeline.label: The Willows published
timeline.detail: In The Listener and Other Stories, the collection that made his reputation.

timeline.label: Blackwood's John Silence published
timeline.detail: The psychic-detective stories that sold well and that Blackwood later thought less of than this one.

timeline.label: Blackwood's The Wendigo published
timeline.detail: Its companion piece, doing for the Canadian bush what this does for the Danube.

timeline.label: Lovecraft calls it the finest weird tale
timeline.detail: In Supernatural Horror in Literature he names The Willows the finest weird tale he has read.

timeline.label: Blackwood becomes a BBC broadcaster
timeline.detail: He became famous all over again as a broadcaster telling ghost stories on the BBC.

timeline.label: Blackwood dies
timeline.detail: He died on 10 December 1951. The story has stayed in print in horror anthologies ever since.

books.title: The Wind in the Willows
books.author: Kenneth Grahame
books.written: Out of bedtime stories and letters sent to the author’s son in 1907

timeline.label: Kenneth Grahame born in Edinburgh
timeline.detail: He was brought up largely by relatives in Berkshire after his mother’s death, on the stretch of the Thames the book keeps returning to.

timeline.label: Grahame enters the Bank of England
timeline.detail: He worked there for nearly thirty years while publishing essays and stories in his own time.

timeline.label: The Golden Age published
timeline.detail: Sketches of childhood seen from the child’s side; Dream Days followed in 1898.

timeline.label: Grahame becomes Secretary of the Bank of England
timeline.detail: The most senior post he held, and the one he resigned a few months before the novel appeared.

timeline.label: The Motor Car Act
timeline.detail: Registration, driving licences and a twenty-mile-an-hour limit — the legal background to Toad’s career on the road.

timeline.label: Grahame's story letters to his son Alastair
timeline.detail: Grahame sent his young son a series of animal-story letters; fifteen survive in the Bodleian with manuscript material for the novel.

timeline.label: Published by Methuen
timeline.detail: Grahame resigned from the Bank in June; Methuen published The Wind in the Willows on 8 October.

timeline.label: Alastair Grahame dies at Oxford
timeline.detail: The son the stories were first told to; he was nineteen.

timeline.label: A. A. Milne’s Toad of Toad Hall staged
timeline.detail: The dramatisation keeps the Toad plot and drops the chapters that have no jokes in them, a division most adaptations have followed.

timeline.label: E. H. Shepard illustrates the book
timeline.detail: His drawings fixed the appearance of the four animals for most readers; the 1908 first edition had a frontispiece and nothing else.

timeline.label: Grahame dies at Pangbourne
timeline.detail: He is buried at Oxford, beside Alastair.

timeline.label: Robert Greene's Pandosto published
timeline.detail: The prose romance Shakespeare follows closely, and whose jealous king kills himself at the end.

timeline.label: Greene dies, having attacked Shakespeare in print
timeline.detail: The pamphlet that calls him an upstart crow appeared in the same year; twenty years later Shakespeare took Greene's plot.

timeline.label: The Winter's Tale most likely written
timeline.detail: Usually dated 1609–11, among the late plays and close to Cymbeline and The Tempest.

timeline.label: Simon Forman sees the play at the Globe
timeline.detail: His notebook entry of 15 May records the plot, the bear and, at length, Autolycus; the moral he draws is to beware of trusting feigned beggars.

timeline.label: Played at court for Princess Elizabeth's wedding festivities
timeline.detail: The King's Men gave a long series of plays for the marriage of James's daughter, and this was among them.

timeline.label: Jonson mocks plays of this kind in Bartholomew Fair
timeline.detail: The induction to Bartholomew Fair jeers at plays full of servant-monsters and drolleries — a contemporary judgement on exactly this kind of writing.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, printed last among the comedies and generally thought to have been set from a scribe's transcript.

timeline.label: Garrick's Florizel and Perdita
timeline.detail: An adaptation that kept the pastoral and cut most of the first three acts, and held the stage for decades.

timeline.label: The full play returns to the London stage
timeline.detail: The nineteenth century restored the tragic first half, and the statue scene became one of the great set pieces of the English theatre.

books.title: The Woman in White
books.author: Wilkie Collins
books.written: Begun 15 August 1859; the manuscript finished 26 July 1860, with the serial still running

timeline.label: Wilkie Collins born in London
timeline.detail: Son of the landscape painter William Collins, and trained for the law before he gave it up for fiction.

timeline.label: Collins meets Dickens
timeline.detail: An amateur theatrical brings them together, and Dickens’s magazines become Collins’s main platform for the next decade.

timeline.label: Composition begins
timeline.detail: Collins started writing on 15 August at Broadstairs, with no complete manuscript and a serial slot already booked.

timeline.label: Serialisation starts
timeline.detail: The first instalment appeared on 26 November in All the Year Round and, the same week, in Harper’s Weekly in New York.

timeline.label: The manuscript is finished
timeline.detail: Collins completed it on 26 July, while the serial was still running; the British serial ended on 25 August.

timeline.label: First English book edition
timeline.detail: Three volumes, in the expensive format that circulating libraries preferred.

timeline.label: The revised one-volume text
timeline.detail: Collins corrected the chronology and added a dated preface; this is the text most modern editions follow.

timeline.label: Collins's The Moonstone published
timeline.detail: Collins uses the same method again — a case assembled from the statements of people who each saw one part of it.

timeline.label: Collins’s own stage version
timeline.detail: He dramatised the novel himself, part of a long effort to keep control of a story that was being adapted without him.

timeline.label: Collins dies
timeline.detail: He had published more than twenty novels, and the sensation novel had long since been absorbed into the detective story.

timeline.label: Warner Bros. film
timeline.detail: Directed by Peter Godfrey, with Eleanor Parker in the double role of Laura and Anne, which is how the cinema usually solves the resemblance.

timeline.label: BBC television serial
timeline.detail: A serial version with room to keep the narrators separate, which is how the novel’s documentary structure survives adaptation.

timeline.label: BBC television film
timeline.detail: A single-film adaptation that compresses the eleven narratives into one line of action, as most screen versions do.

books.title: The Yellow Wall-Paper and The Giant Wistaria
books.author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
books.written: The Yellow Wall-Paper in two days at Pasadena in June 1890; The Giant Wistaria a little earlier

timeline.label: Charlotte Perkins born in Hartford
timeline.detail: Her father left the family early; she grew up moving between relatives, with an education she largely arranged herself.

timeline.label: Charlotte Perkins marries Charles Walter Stetson
timeline.detail: She had hesitated for two years, telling him she doubted she was fit for marriage.

timeline.label: Gilman's daughter Katharine born; depression follows
timeline.detail: The illness the story draws on began within weeks of the birth.

timeline.label: Gilman undergoes S. Weir Mitchell's rest cure
timeline.detail: Treated in Philadelphia by S. Weir Mitchell and sent home told to live as domestic a life as possible and never to touch pen, brush or pencil again.

timeline.label: Gilman leaves her marriage and moves to Pasadena
timeline.detail: Separation and a move to Pasadena, where she began to write and lecture; the divorce followed in 1894.

timeline.label: The Yellow Wall-Paper written
timeline.detail: Composed in June, in two days, and turned down by the Atlantic Monthly's editor, who said he could not forgive himself for making others as miserable as it had made him.

timeline.label: The Giant Wistaria printed
timeline.detail: Published in The New England Magazine in June, seven months before its companion piece.

timeline.label: The Yellow Wall-Paper printed
timeline.detail: In The New England Magazine for January, with illustrations; some readers wrote in to ask whether such a case could be real.

timeline.label: The first book edition
timeline.detail: Issued by Small, Maynard & Co. in Boston, the text behind most later American reprints.

timeline.label: Gilman's essay 'Why I Wrote The Yellow Wallpaper?'
timeline.detail: In her own magazine The Forerunner, Gilman said she had sent the story to Mitchell and heard that he had altered his treatment — an account no other source confirms.

timeline.label: Gilman dies in Pasadena
timeline.detail: Facing inoperable cancer, she ended her own life, having written that a last duty is to choose one's own way out.

timeline.label: The Feminist Press reprint
timeline.detail: Elaine Hedges's edition returned the story to print and to teaching, where it has stayed.

timeline.label: Magna Carta is agreed at Runnymede
timeline.detail: In June, on the meadows between Staines and Windsor. Jerome has King John rowed to the island opposite and sign it there, and declines to say which side of the water is right.

timeline.label: Jerome Klapka Jerome is born in Walsall
timeline.detail: On 2 May. He grew up in poverty in east London, and worked as a railway clerk, actor, schoolmaster and journalist before he made a living from books.

timeline.label: HMS Pinafore opens in London
timeline.detail: Gilbert and Sullivan’s comic opera, whose First Lord’s song Harris muddles with the Judge’s song from Trial by Jury in chapter VIII. The First Lord was created by George Grossmith, co-author of The Diary of a Nobody.

timeline.label: Parliament passes the Thames Preservation Act
timeline.detail: Meant to keep the river open for pleasure boating as riverside owners tried to fence off banks and backwaters, the grievance behind J.’s rage at notice-boards and chains.

timeline.label: Jerome's Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow published
timeline.detail: Jerome’s book of comic essays, named on the title page of Three Men in a Boat as his earlier work. Its manner, reflective and self-mocking, is the narrator’s voice here.

timeline.label: Jerome marries Georgina Marris
timeline.detail: In June. The couple spent their honeymoon on the Thames, and the serial began that autumn.

timeline.label: The serial begins in Home Chimes
timeline.detail: Running from September 1888 to June 1889, according to the Jerome K. Jerome Society’s bibliography, before the book appeared.

timeline.label: J. W. Arrowsmith publishes the book in Bristol
timeline.detail: In August, with illustrations by A. Frederics and a preface praising its hopeless and incurable veracity. The same firm published The Diary of a Nobody three years later.

timeline.label: Three Men on the Bummel, the sequel, published
timeline.detail: The sequel sends J., George and Harris on a bicycling tour of Germany.

timeline.label: Arrowsmith advertises 202,000 copies in twenty years
timeline.detail: A publisher’s figure for copies produced, not an audited sales total, and it could not include the unauthorised American editions.

timeline.label: Jerome publishes My Life and Times
timeline.detail: The memoir in which he recalls the book’s origins and its hostile reviews. Some of the reviews he quotes have not been traced to their original issues, so his account is best read as recollection.

timeline.label: Jerome dies at Northampton
timeline.detail: On 14 June, after a stroke suffered on a motoring tour.

timeline.label: Ken Annakin’s film
timeline.detail: A British colour film with David Tomlinson, Jimmy Edwards and Laurence Harvey as the three men.

timeline.label: BBC television adaptation by Tom Stoppard
timeline.detail: Directed by Stephen Frears, with Michael Palin, Tim Curry and Stephen Moore in the boat.

timeline.label: North's Plutarch published in English
timeline.detail: The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romanes, where the lives of Antony and Alcibiades carry the few paragraphs about Timon and both of the epitaphs.

timeline.label: An academic Timon comedy circulates in manuscript
timeline.detail: An anonymous English play on the same story, with a mock banquet of painted stones, survives from about this date. Whether Shakespeare knew it is disputed.

timeline.label: The play written, probably with Thomas Middleton
timeline.detail: No payment, performance or Stationers' Register entry fixes the date. The verse and the vocabulary sit close to King Lear.

timeline.label: Printed in the First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, set between Romeo and Juliet and Julius Caesar in a gap that opened when the printers ran into difficulty over Troilus and Cressida.

timeline.label: Shadwell's The History of Timon of Athens, the Man-Hater
timeline.detail: An adaptation that gave Timon two women, one faithful and one false, and kept the story on the London stage for most of a century.

timeline.label: Richard Cumberland's version at Drury Lane
timeline.detail: Another rewriting, this time providing Timon with a daughter to be married to Alcibiades.

timeline.label: Samuel Phelps stages it at Sadler's Wells
timeline.detail: Close to Shakespeare's text, and the first London production in generations that was not an adaptation.

timeline.label: Paul Scofield plays Timon for the Royal Shakespeare Company
timeline.detail: Directed by John Schlesinger at Stratford, and the production that brought the play back into the regular repertory.

timeline.label: Richard Pasco plays Timon for the RSC
timeline.detail: One of a run of postwar revivals that treated the play as a study of patronage and money instead of an unfinished curiosity.

timeline.label: Gregory Doran directs Michael Pennington at the RSC
timeline.detail: Staged in a world of corporate hospitality, with the first banquet played as a company party.

timeline.label: The New Oxford Shakespeare prints it as a collaboration
timeline.detail: Timon of Athens appears under two names, Shakespeare's and Middleton's, after decades of stylistic and textual work.

timeline.label: Simon Godwin directs Kathryn Hunter as Timon
timeline.detail: At the RSC, with gold as the visible substance of the first half and a set that decayed as the money went.

timeline.label: Ovid completes the Metamorphoses
timeline.detail: Book VI tells of Tereus, Philomela and the weaving that exposes him, and of the meal Procne serves afterwards. Shakespeare puts the book itself on stage in Act IV.

timeline.label: Seneca His Tenne Tragedies printed in English
timeline.detail: Thomas Newton's collection put Thyestes and its banquet of children into the hands of English playwrights and their audiences.

timeline.label: Titus Andronicus written
timeline.detail: Usually dated to the early 1590s, and often called Shakespeare's first tragedy. Some arguments for an earlier start rest on Jonson's later joke about the play's ageing admirers.

timeline.label: Performed at the Rose on 24 January
timeline.detail: Philip Henslowe recorded the takings for Titus & ondronicus in his account book, marking it as a new play for Sussex's Men.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register and printed
timeline.detail: John Danter entered A Noble Roman Historye of Tytus Andronicus on 6 February and printed the quarto for Edward White and Thomas Millington. It is the first printing of any Shakespeare play, and one copy survives.

timeline.label: Second quarto
timeline.detail: James Roberts printed Q2 for Edward White; Edward Allde printed a third quarto for White in 1611. Both show the play still selling twenty years on.

timeline.label: Jonson jokes about it in Bartholomew Fair
timeline.detail: The Induction mocks playgoers who still call Titus Andronicus the best thing going, saying their judgement has stood still for twenty-five or thirty years.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The play is printed among the tragedies, from a copy of Q3 marked up against a playhouse manuscript. The Folio alone prints the fly scene at 3.2.

timeline.label: Ravenscroft's adaptation
timeline.detail: Edward Ravenscroft rewrote it as Titus Andronicus, or The Rape of Lavinia, and his preface began the long tradition of doubting that Shakespeare wrote all of it.

timeline.label: Peter Brook directs Olivier and Vivien Leigh
timeline.detail: At Stratford, with stylised blood and Laurence Olivier as Titus. The production is generally credited with making the play stageable again after two centuries of embarrassment.

timeline.label: Deborah Warner at the Swan
timeline.detail: With Brian Cox as Titus, Estelle Kohler as Tamora and Sonia Ritter as Lavinia. The staging let the play be funny, and found that the laughter made the horror worse.

timeline.label: Julie Taymor's film Titus
timeline.detail: Anthony Hopkins and Jessica Lange, in a design that mixes Roman architecture with twentieth-century fascism. Harry Lennix's Aaron brought the part to a wide audience.

timeline.label: Chaucer finishes Troilus and Criseyde
timeline.detail: The long poem that gives Shakespeare the lovers, the uncle and the exchange, and treats all three with a tenderness the play removes.

timeline.label: Caxton prints the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye
timeline.detail: The first book printed in English, and the source for most of the war material, including the embassy, the duel and Hector's death.

timeline.label: Lydgate's Troy Book printed
timeline.detail: Pynson's edition of a poem written a century earlier for Prince Hal; behind the play's Trojan council and the stress on Hector's courtesy.

timeline.label: Chapman's Seven Books of the Iliads
timeline.detail: The first substantial Homer in English, which put the Greek heroes in front of a London reader at the moment the play was being planned.

timeline.label: A rival Troilus for the Admiral's Men
timeline.detail: Henslowe pays Dekker and Chettle for a play on the same story; a fragment of its plot survives, and nothing of its text.

timeline.label: Probably written
timeline.detail: The usual dating puts it with Hamlet and the other plays of the turn of the century, though no record fixes the year or a first performance.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register
timeline.detail: James Roberts enters it on 7 February as acted by the Lord Chamberlain's men, and then does not print it.

timeline.label: Quarto printed, in two states
timeline.detail: Bonian and Walley print it; some copies advertise performance at the Globe, others replace the title page and add a preface claiming it was never staged.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the tragedies but left out of the catalogue at the front of the volume, and carrying the Prologue for the first time.

timeline.label: Dryden's Truth Found Too Late
timeline.detail: A rewriting that makes Cressida faithful and has her kill herself to prove it, and keeps the play off the stage in its own form for two centuries.

timeline.label: William Poel stages it in London
timeline.detail: The Elizabethan Stage Society production at King's Hall, Covent Garden, the first professional performance of Shakespeare's text in England since the seventeenth century.

timeline.label: Michael Macowan's modern dress production
timeline.detail: At the Westminster Theatre, with the Greeks in service uniform and Thersites as a war correspondent, opening as the Munich crisis broke.

timeline.label: Peter Hall and John Barton at Stratford
timeline.detail: Played on a square of sand with the armies half naked; the production that established the play in the modern repertory.

timeline.label: Barnabe Riche's Farewell to Military Profession
timeline.detail: Contains 'Of Apolonius and Silla', the twin-and-disguise tale that is the play's chief source.

timeline.label: The play is most likely written
timeline.detail: Dated by its style and by the fact that it was already being performed early in 1602.

timeline.label: Performed at Middle Temple Hall
timeline.detail: On 2 February, recorded in the diary of the law student John Manningham — the earliest surviving notice of the play.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies as Twelfe Night, Or what you will; there is no earlier text.

timeline.label: Harley Granville-Barker's Savoy production
timeline.detail: A fast, uncut staging on a simple set that helped end the tradition of heavy Victorian scenery in Shakespeare.

timeline.label: John Barton's production for the Royal Shakespeare Company
timeline.detail: An autumnal, melancholy reading that shaped how the play was staged for a generation.

timeline.label: Trevor Nunn's film
timeline.detail: A screen version that opens with the shipwreck and gives the Malvolio plot its full weight.

timeline.label: An all-male staging at Shakespeare's Globe
timeline.detail: Original-practices costume and casting, with Mark Rylance as Olivia, revived a decade later in the West End and on Broadway.

timeline.label: Harriet Beecher born in Litchfield, Connecticut
timeline.detail: Into a famous clerical family; her father Lyman Beecher and several brothers were preachers.

timeline.label: The Beechers move to Cincinnati
timeline.detail: Eighteen years living on the Ohio, across the river from a slave state, gave her most of what she knew at first hand.

timeline.label: Marriage to Calvin Stowe
timeline.detail: A biblical scholar; the couple later moved to Brunswick, Maine, where the novel was begun.

timeline.label: The Fugitive Slave Act
timeline.detail: Part of the Compromise of 1850, it required citizens of free states to assist in recapture and is the immediate provocation for the book.

timeline.label: Serialisation begins in The National Era
timeline.detail: From June, in an abolitionist weekly in Washington; the story ran far beyond its planned length.

timeline.label: Published in two volumes by John P. Jewett
timeline.detail: It sold on a scale no American novel had reached before, and was pirated and translated across Europe within the year.

timeline.label: The first stage versions appear
timeline.detail: Unlicensed dramatisations began at once; the 'Tom shows' outlived the book's reputation and coarsened everything in it.

timeline.label: Stowe publishes A Key to Uncle Tom's Cabin
timeline.detail: Stowe answered accusations of invention by publishing the court records, advertisements and narratives behind her scenes.

timeline.label: The Dred Scott decision
timeline.detail: The Supreme Court held that a black American could not be a citizen, hardening the argument the novel had entered.

timeline.label: The American Civil War begins
timeline.detail: The story that Lincoln greeted Stowe as the little woman who started the war is undocumented and long-lived.

timeline.label: The Thirteenth Amendment
timeline.detail: Slavery abolished in the United States, thirteen years after the book appeared.

timeline.label: Stowe dies at Hartford, Connecticut
timeline.detail: By then the novel's stage afterlife had largely replaced the book in the public mind.

timeline.label: Thomas More born in London
timeline.detail: Son of John More, a lawyer who later became a judge of the King’s Bench. The year usually given is 1478.

timeline.label: A page in Cardinal Morton’s household, c. 1490
timeline.detail: As a boy More waited at the table of John Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury and Chancellor, whom Hythloday describes in Book I.

timeline.label: The Cornish rising crushed
timeline.detail: Hythloday says he was in England ‘not long after the rebellion in the West was suppressed’, which places Morton’s dinner in about this year.

timeline.label: Vespucci’s voyages in print
timeline.detail: An account of Amerigo Vespucci’s four voyages was printed at Saint-Dié with a new map of the world. Hythloday claims to have sailed on three of them.

timeline.label: The Praise of Folly printed
timeline.detail: Erasmus wrote it in More’s London house and titled it Moriae Encomium, a pun on his friend’s name. Utopia comes from the same circle and the same habit of serious joking.

timeline.label: Machiavelli writes The Prince
timeline.detail: Another out-of-office official’s advice to rulers, taking the opposite view of how far a counsellor should accommodate power. It was not printed until 1532.

timeline.label: Begun during the embassy to Flanders
timeline.detail: In May More went with Cuthbert Tunstall to negotiate with the commissioners of Charles, Prince of Castile, and in Antwerp became friends with Peter Giles. The island of Book II was probably written later in the year.

timeline.label: First edition, Louvain
timeline.detail: Printed in Latin by Dirk Martens late in the year, with a woodcut map of the island, a Utopian alphabet and letters and verses by More’s friends.

timeline.label: Revised editions printed at Basel
timeline.detail: Johann Froben printed revised editions at Basel, with woodcuts by Ambrosius Holbein.

timeline.label: More becomes Lord Chancellor
timeline.detail: He succeeded Wolsey in October, in the office Morton had held, and resigned in 1532 as Henry VIII moved against the Church.

timeline.label: More executed
timeline.detail: Beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July, having refused to accept Henry VIII as supreme head of the church in England.

timeline.label: The first English translation
timeline.detail: Ralph Robinson’s version was printed in the reign of Edward VI, sixteen years after More’s death.

timeline.label: Burnet’s translation
timeline.detail: Gilbert Burnet, later Bishop of Salisbury, translated the book soon after the execution of his friend Lord William Russell. His English is the text quoted here.

timeline.label: More declared a saint
timeline.detail: Pope Pius XI canonised More, with John Fisher, four hundred years after their deaths.

timeline.label: H. G. Wells born at Bromley
timeline.detail: He later trained in science in South Kensington under T. H. Huxley.

timeline.label: Schiaparelli maps the canali of Mars
timeline.detail: The Italian word for channels was widely read in English as canals, and the idea of Martian engineering entered popular astronomy.

timeline.label: Percival Lowell opens his observatory at Flagstaff
timeline.detail: Built largely to study Mars; the novel opens with a light seen on the planet at the 1894 opposition.

timeline.label: The Time Machine published
timeline.detail: Wells's first scientific romance, and the beginning of four years that also produced Moreau, The Invisible Man and this book.

timeline.label: The Island of Doctor Moreau published
timeline.detail: Its interest in the boundary between men and animals runs straight into the artilleryman's argument about ants.

timeline.label: Serialised in Pearson's Magazine
timeline.detail: British readers met the invasion in monthly instalments; an American serial ran in Cosmopolitan.

timeline.label: First book edition, William Heinemann
timeline.detail: Harper and Brothers issued the American book edition the same year.

timeline.label: Orson Welles broadcasts the story on CBS
timeline.detail: Howard Koch's adaptation moved the first landing to Grovers Mill, New Jersey, and used the form of a news bulletin.

timeline.label: Wells dies in London
timeline.detail: By then he was known as much for his histories and political writing as for the scientific romances.

timeline.label: George Pal's film released
timeline.detail: Directed by Byron Haskin, it relocated the invasion to mid-century America and replaced the tripods with flying machines.

timeline.label: Jeff Wayne's musical version released
timeline.detail: A concept album narrated by Richard Burton, which kept the novel's structure of a witness reporting after the event.

timeline.label: Steven Spielberg's film released
timeline.detail: Refocused on one family in flight, and on the refugee traffic that occupies the brother's chapters.

books.title: White Fang
books.author: Jack London
books.written: c. 1904–05, in California, as a deliberate companion to The Call of the Wild

timeline.label: Jack London born in San Francisco
timeline.detail: He grew up poor around Oakland and the bay, the city whose slums he gives to Jim Hall.

timeline.label: London goes north to the Klondike
timeline.detail: He wintered in the Yukon in the first season of the rush and came home the following summer with scurvy and notebooks rather than gold.

timeline.label: The novel's only date: Fort Yukon, summer 1898
timeline.detail: White Fang reaches Fort Yukon in the summer of 1898, with thousands of gold-hunters going upriver to Dawson — the only calendar date in the book.

timeline.label: The Call of the Wild published
timeline.detail: Its success fixed London’s public identity and created the appetite for a second dog book.

timeline.label: London buys land at Glen Ellen
timeline.detail: The beginning of the Sonoma ranch where he lived for the rest of his life; the novel’s Californian chapters were written by a man settling into the country himself.

timeline.label: White Fang serialised and published
timeline.detail: Six monthly instalments in Outing from May to October, then the Macmillan book with colour plates by Charles Livingston Bull.

timeline.label: Roosevelt attacks the ‘nature fakers’
timeline.detail: The President, in a magazine interview, singled out the fight between the bulldog and the wolf-dog as the kind of thing no naturalist could believe.

timeline.label: London replies in ‘The Other Animals’
timeline.detail: Published in Collier’s in September, the essay defends his dogs as creatures of instinct and simple reasoning rather than of human thought.

timeline.label: London dies at Glen Ellen
timeline.detail: He was forty, and had published some fifty books in seventeen years.

timeline.label: First film adaptation
timeline.detail: A silent feature built around the dog star Strongheart, beginning a long line of screen versions.

timeline.label: A Soviet film version
timeline.detail: London’s standing as a socialist author made him one of the most widely read Americans in the Soviet Union, and the novel was filmed there soon after the war.

timeline.label: The Disney live-action film
timeline.detail: It enlarges the human story, gives the dog a young prospector for a companion and leaves out California and Jim Hall altogether.

timeline.label: An animated feature
timeline.detail: A French-made animated version told largely from the animal’s side, released internationally by a streaming service.

timeline.label: Emily Brontë born at Thornton
timeline.detail: The fifth of six children; the family moved to Haworth parsonage two years later.

timeline.label: Emily sent to school at Cowan Bridge
timeline.detail: Emily went with her sisters to the Clergy Daughters' School, and was withdrawn the following year after Maria and Elizabeth fell fatally ill.

timeline.label: Emily teaches at Law Hill, near Halifax
timeline.detail: Emily taught at a school here for a few months; the district's houses and local histories have often been connected with the novel.

timeline.label: Emily and Charlotte study in Brussels
timeline.detail: Emily and Charlotte studied at the Pensionnat Heger; the French essays Emily wrote there are among the few pieces of her prose outside the novel.

timeline.label: Charlotte finds Emily's poems
timeline.detail: The discovery, against Emily's wishes, led to the sisters' joint volume and to all three attempting novels.

timeline.label: Poems by Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell published
timeline.detail: Published at the sisters' own expense; it sold two copies.

timeline.label: Wuthering Heights published
timeline.detail: Thomas Cautley Newby issued it in December in three volumes, with Anne Brontë's Agnes Grey as the third.

timeline.label: Emily Brontë dies at Haworth
timeline.detail: In December, of consumption, a few months after her brother Branwell and about a year after the novel appeared.

timeline.label: Charlotte Brontë's revised edition
timeline.detail: She corrected the text, thinned Joseph's dialect for southern readers, and added a biographical notice and a preface answering the charge of brutality.

timeline.label: William Wyler's film
timeline.detail: With Laurence Olivier and Merle Oberon; it ends at Catherine's death and omits the second generation entirely, which shaped the popular idea of the book for decades.

timeline.label: Andrea Arnold's film
timeline.detail: Shot on the moors with a Black actor as Heathcliff and almost no score, it returns the novel's questions about race and origin to the foreground.
